items.title: Tumor Treating Fields and Quality of Life Among Patients With Locally Advanced Pancreatic Adenocarcinoma: A Secondary Analysis of a Randomized Clinical Trial.
items.abstract:
IMPORTANCE: The PANOVA-3 trial demonstrated the survival benefit and tolerability of Tumor Treating Fields (TTFields) therapy concomitant with gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel, but understanding the impact of TTFields therapy on quality of life (QoL) and pain is important for clinical decision-making.
OBJECTIVE: To analyze the impact of TTFields therapy concomitant with gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel on QoL and pain outcomes using prospective data from PANOVA-3.
DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: This is a prespecified secondary analysis of PANOVA-3, which was a global, open-label, multicenter, phase 3 randomized clinical trial in adult patients with previously untreated locally advanced unresectable pancreatic adenocarcinoma (LA-PAC). A total of 571 patients were randomized between May 1, 2018, and March 31, 2023, with follow-up completed October 31, 2024. Data analysis was performed from November 2024 to May 2025.
INTERVENTION: Patients were randomized 1:1 to receive either TTFields therapy (150 kHz) with gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel or gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel alone. Nab-paclitaxel (125 mg/m2) and gemcitabine (1000 mg/m2) were administered intravenously on days 1, 8, and 15 of 28-day cycles. Duration of follow-up was 18 months.
MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: QoL was measured using the European Organization for the Research and Treatment of Cancer Core Quality of Life Questionnaire and the 26-item pancreatic cancer module. End points were mean changes from baseline QoL scores, deterioration-free survival of QoL, and time to opioid use. An analysis of pain medication use was performed post hoc.
RESULTS: At baseline, 562 patients (median [IQR] age, 67 [31-90] years; 295 [52.5%] female), including 279 of 285 patients in the TTFields plus gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel arm and 283 of 286 patients in the gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel arm, completed the EORTC QLQ-C30 questionnaire. Global health status was stable during the 26-month follow-up in both study arms. Digestive symptoms, pain, and pancreatic pain were improved from 2 months after treatment initiation throughout treatment and follow-up in the TTFields plus gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel arm. TTFields plus gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel was associated with longer deterioration-free survival for global health status than gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel alone (median [IQR], 7.1 [3.5-14.8] vs 5.7 [2.3-11.5] months; hazard ratio [HR], 0.77; 95% CI, 0.61-0.97; P = .02). Longer deterioration-free survival was also observed for most items on the digestive symptoms scales (indigestion and altered bowel habit were similar between the 2 arms). Median (IQR) deterioration-free survival was significantly longer with TTFields plus gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel for pain (10.1 [4.0-20.9] vs 7.4 [3.5-14.5] months; HR, 0.70; 95% CI, 0.54-0.89; P = .003) and pancreatic pain (14.7 [6.2-46.2] vs 10.2 [5.6-18.2] months; HR, 0.69; 95% CI, 0.52-0.90; P = .006) as was median time to opioid use in the modified intention-to-treat population (9.3 [3.9-18.6] vs 6.7 [1.1-16.3] months; HR, 0.72; 95% CI, 0.55-0.93; P = .01).
CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: This secondary analysis of a randomized clinical trial found that TTFields therapy with gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel improved QoL and provided clinically meaningful benefits in pain outcomes compared with gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel alone. This study's results suggest that TTFields therapy with gemicitabine and nab-paclitaxel is practice-changing for patients with unresectable LA-PAC.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT03377491.

items.title: Depletion of Endogenous IL-18 Suppresses Pancreatic Cancer Progression, Reprograms the Tumor Microenvironment, and Enhances KRAS Inhibitor Efficacy.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND & AIMS: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) exhibits a highly complex tumor microenvironment enriched with both inflammatory and immunosuppressive factors. Interleukin-18 (IL-18), a cytokine of the IL-1 family, is elevated in PDAC and correlates with poor patient outcomes. However, the functional role of IL-18 in PDAC progression and immune regulation remains poorly defined.
METHODS: We generated genetically engineered mouse models with IL-18 depletion in the context of spontaneous PDAC development. Single-cell RNA-sequencing and functional assays were used to analyze PDAC progression, macrophage phenotypes, and cancer cell-macrophage interactions. Mechanistic studies were performed to determine the effects of IL-18 on STAT1 signaling and CD47 expression. The role of IL-18 in therapeutic response was evaluated using KRAS inhibitor (KRASi) treatment models.
RESULTS: Elevated IL-18 expression correlated with poor patient survival. Genetic depletion of IL-18 significantly suppressed spontaneous PDAC progression and prolonged survival in mice. Mechanistically, IL-18 promoted cancer cell survival by activating STAT1-dependent CD47 expression, thereby impairing macrophage-mediated phagocytosis of cancer cells. In addition, IL-18 depletion reshaped the tumor immune microenvironment by enriching macrophage populations with enhanced antigen-presenting and phagocytic phenotypes characterized by increased MHCII and CD11c expression. Notably, KRAS inhibitor treatment further increased IL-18 expression in PDAC cells, whereas IL-18 depletion enhanced macrophage-mediated clearance of KRASi-treated cancer cells and improved therapeutic efficacy.
CONCLUSIONS: IL-18 promotes pancreatic cancer progression by enabling cancer cell survival and immune evasion through macrophage reprogramming. Targeting IL-18 may represent a therapeutic strategy to enhance macrophage-mediated anti-tumor immunity and improve responses to KRAS inhibitor therapies in PDAC.

items.title: Prognostic factors for resectable pancreatic adenocarcinoma: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Prognostic stratification after curative-intent resection for pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains challenging. We performed a systematic review and meta-analysis to identify prognostic factors associated with overall survival (OS) in resected PDAC.
METHODS: PubMed, Embase, Web of Science and the Cochrane Library were searched for studies reporting hazard ratios (HRs) for OS after PDAC resection. Observational studies and randomized trials reporting univariable or multivariable HRs for clinicopathologic and treatment variables were eligible, regardless of treatment sequence. Pooled HRs with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were estimated using fixed- or random-effects models according to heterogeneity, and multivariable estimates were synthesized when available.
RESULTS: Fifty-two studies (79,446 patients) were included. In univariable analyses, older age, male sex, elevated preoperative CA19-9 and CEA, higher NLR and CRP/Alb, pancreaticoduodenectomy (PD) vs. distal pancreatectomy (DP), vascular/perineural invasion, positive resection margin, poor differentiation, advanced T stage, and node-positive disease were associated with worse OS, whereas postoperative adjuvant chemotherapy was associated with improved OS. In pooled multivariable analyses, older age (HR 2.17), male sex (HR 1.62), PD vs. DP (HR 1.76), high CA19-9 (HR 1.63), elevated NLR (HR 1.62), increased CRP/Alb (HR 2.05), vascular invasion (HR 1.54), positive resection margin (HR 1.73), poor histologic grade (HR 1.63), advanced T stage (HR 1.74), and node-positive disease (HR 1.68) were associated with worse OS, while adjuvant chemotherapy was consistently associated with improved survival (HR 0.52). Preoperative CEA and perineural invasion did not retain statistical significance in pooled multivariable analyses.
CONCLUSIONS: In resected PDAC, prognosis appears to reflect not only anatomic stage but also pathological, biological, host-related, and treatment-related factors. These findings support a more integrated postoperative risk-stratification framework beyond anatomic staging alone, which may help identify high-risk patients and inform postoperative management.

items.title: Postoperative Tumor-Informed Circulating Tumor DNA Status for Molecular Residual Disease Detection After Curative-Intent Resection of Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) frequently recurs after curative-intent resection, and conventional imaging and CA19-9 have limited sensitivity for detecting molecular residual disease (MRD). Tumor-informed circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) may identify postoperative MRD, although the evidence is limited and heterogeneous.
METHODS: PubMed, Scopus, and Embase were searched from inception to July 9, 2026, following PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Eligible studies compared postoperative tumor-informed ctDNA-positive and ctDNA-negative patients after curative-intent treatment of pancreatic cancer for recurrence, survival, or lead time outcomes. Random-effects models were used to pool risk ratios (RRs) and hazard ratios (HRs). Heterogeneity, leave-one-out sensitivity, prespecified subgroups, ROBINS-I risk of bias, and GRADE certainty were assessed.
RESULTS: Five observational cohorts contributed 237 patients to the radiological recurrence comparison (84 ctDNA-positive and 153 ctDNA-negative). Postoperative ctDNA positivity was associated with increased radiological recurrence (RR 2.50; 95% CI 1.90-3.28; I²=20%), poorer disease-free survival (HR 8.11; 95% CI 3.51-18.73; I²=45%), and poorer overall survival (HR 5.15; 95% CI 2.67-9.94; I²=0%). The direction of the associations persisted in the reported leave-one-out assessments. Recurrence risk was higher in both the early-MRD/landmark and surveillance subgroups, with no statistically significant subgroup difference (P = 0.17).
CONCLUSION: Postoperative tumor-informed ctDNA positivity was associated with an increased recurrence risk and inferior survival after curative-intent PDAC treatment, although a negative result did not reliably exclude residual disease. Prospective interventional studies are needed before ctDNA-guided surveillance or treatment modifications can be recommended for routine practice.

items.title: Geriatric nutritional risk index as a potential prognostic indicator in pancreatic cancer: evidence from a systematic review and meta-analysis.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Malnutrition is highly prevalent among patients with pancreatic cancer and has a substantial impact on prognosis, treatment tolerability, and quality of life. However, the prognostic significance of the Geriatric Nutritional Risk Index (GNRI), a simple and objective tool for assessing nutritional status, in pancreatic cancer remains incompletely characterized, and the available evidence has not been comprehensively synthesized.
AIMS: Therefore, this study aimed to systematically evaluate the association between GNRI and overall survival in patients with pancreatic cancer.
METHODS: A systematic literature search of PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science, and Scopus was conducted (PROSPERO: CRD420251177304) to identify prospective and retrospective observational studies published up to November 2025 that reported quantitative data on the association between GNRI and survival outcomes in patients with pancreatic cancer. Eligible studies were included in a systematic review, and those meeting predefined criteria were pooled in a meta-analysis.
RESULTS: Eighteen observational studies were included, of which 13 were eligible for meta-analysis. High nutritional risk according to the GNRI was associated with significantly worse overall survival (pooled HR = 1.79; 95% CI: 1.42-2.26; I² = 66.0%). Subgroup analyses showed stronger effects in univariate analyses, while attenuated associations were observed in multivariable-adjusted studies; reconstructed hazard ratios were larger than those directly reported. Trim-and-fill analysis yielded similar results (adjusted HR = 1.58; 95% CI: 1.25-2.00).
CONCLUSIONS: GNRI may serve as a potential prognostic indicator of overall survival in patients with pancreatic cancer and a clinically useful screening tool for risk stratification.

items.title: Metro-Pancreas Stratifies Survival After Neoadjuvant Chemotherapy and Surgery for Resectable Pancreatic Cancer.
items.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To assess the prognostic utility of the Metro-Pancreas framework in resectable pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) treated with neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NAT) and resection.
SUMMARY BACKGROUND DATA: Upfront surgery and NAT are options in anatomically resectable PDAC. Metro-Pancreas combines tumor size and CA 19-9 to stratify prognosis after upfront resection, but its applicability after NAT is unknown.
METHODS: We analyzed 623 patients with nonmetastatic, anatomically resectable PDAC who underwent NAT followed by resection from 5 institutions (2016-2024). Metro-Pancreas classification (IN/OUT) was determined by tumor size and CA19-9 levels. Treatment response followed NCCN 2026 definition based on radiologic and biochemical changes. Postoperative disease-free survival (DFS) and overall survival (OS) were evaluated.
RESULTS: At diagnosis, 263 patients (42.2%) were Metro-Pancreas OUT and had shorter postoperative DFS (13.3 vs. 16.7 mo; P=0.003) and OS (29.5 vs. 34.8 mo; P=0.006) than Metro-Pancreas IN patients. After NAT, 71.9% of OUT patients were reclassified as IN, while 5.0% of initially IN patients became OUT. Among baseline OUT patients, 35.7% had significant response, 46.0% had minimal response, and 18.3% had progression. Prognostic separation was greater at Metro-Pancreas restaging (DFS: 7.7 vs. 17.3 mo; OS: 15.8 vs. 36.7 mo; both P=0.001). Patients reclassified from OUT to IN had postoperative DFS and OS comparable to those initially IN (P=0.806 and P=0.631, respectively).
CONCLUSIONS: Among patients undergoing resection after NAT, Metro-Pancreas stratified prognosis at diagnosis and more effectively at restaging. Reclassification from OUT to IN was associated with favorable postoperative survival, supporting dynamic prognostic reassessment in the neoadjuvant setting.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence-Assisted 4D Dynamic Long-Axial PET Imaging for the Detection of Early Pancreatic Cancer Lesions
items.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is associated with a poor prognosis, and early detection of pancreatic lesions is of great importance for improving patient outcomes. In this study, whole-body imaging with FDG and FAPI will be used to visualize the early development of pancreatic cancer lesions from multiple perspectives, including glucose metabolism, tumor fibrotic stroma, and integrin receptor expression. Furthermore, leveraging the advantages of four-dimensional dynamic long-axial PET imaging, artificial intelligence-assisted lesion detection and analysis will be performed to characterize lesions and differentiate between benign and malignant lesions. The imaging findings will subsequently be compared with postoperative histopathological results to evaluate the diagnostic performance of the proposed imaging approaches.

items.title: Iparomlimab and Tuvonralimab Injection （QL1706）Combined With Chemotherapy (AG) and SBRT as First-Line Treatment for Locally Advanced Pancreatic Cancer
items.abstract:
The goal of this clinical trial is to learn if the study drug QL1706 (iparomlimab and tuvonralimab injection) works to treat locally advanced pancreatic cancer in adults when it is given together with chemotherapy and Stereotactic radiotherapy. It will also learn about the safety of this combination treatment.

Around 37 adults aged 18 to 75 who have pancreatic cancer that has grown into nearby tissue and cannot be removed by surgery, but has not spread to other parts of the body, and who have not yet received any treatment for it, will take part in this study.

The main questions it aims to answer are:

Does the combination of QL1706, chemotherapy and radiation make the tumor shrink or stop growing, making it suitable for surgery? How long do participants live without their cancer getting worse, and how long do they live overall? What medical problems do participants have when taking this combination treatment? All participants in this study will receive the same treatment. There is no placebo (a look-alike substance that contains no drug) and no comparison group. Researchers will compare the results of participants in this study with the results usually seen in people who receive chemotherapy alone, to see if adding QL1706 and radiation helps.

Participants will:

Receive QL1706 through a vein (by intravenous infusion) once every 3 weeks Receive 2 chemotherapy drugs through a vein on days 1 and 8 of every 3-week cycle, for 2 cycles. The 2 drugs are gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel Then receive 5 doses of focused radiation therapy to the pancreas, given about every other day over about 2 weeks, together with 2 more cycles of QL1706 and chemotherapy. Participants whose cancer gets worse during treatment will stop this part of the study Have CT or MRI scans every 6 weeks so the researchers can see whether the cancer has shrunk Have blood tests, physical examinations and other checkups during treatment Be reviewed by a team of pancreatic cancer specialists to see if surgery to remove the tumor is possible. Participants who can have surgery will have the surgery and then 2 to 4 more cycles of QL1706 and chemotherapy. Participants who cannot have surgery, and whose cancer has not grown, will keep receiving QL1706 and chemotherapy until their cancer gets worse, the treatment becomes too hard to tolerate, or they are no longer able to take part Tell the study team about any medical problems they have, which will be recorded throughout the study.

items.title: Robotic pancreatic enucleation versus laparoscopic pancreatic enucleation: a meta-analysis.
items.abstract: Pancreatic enucleation (PE) is an operation that spares pancreatic parenchyma and thereby preserves glandular function, and it is now widely favoured for benign and low-grade malignant pancreatic neoplasms. Whether adding robotic assistance brings benefit beyond the standard laparoscopic route, however, remains an open question. This meta-analysis therefore contrasted robotic pancreatic enucleation (RPE) with laparoscopic pancreatic enucleation (LPE) with respect to perioperative efficacy and safety. Records of cohort studies that contrasted RPE with LPE were retrieved from the Cochrane Library, PubMed, the Wanfang, Embase and China National Knowledge Infrastructure, covering each database from inception to 1 September 2026. Two investigators working in duplicate screened the records, extracted the data and rated methodological quality with the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS). R 4.5.3 with the meta package was used for pooling; mean differences (MDs) and risk ratios (RRs) were presented with their 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Publication-bias and sensitivity analyses were omitted because fewer than 10 eligible studies were available. Five studies met the eligibility criteria (each scoring NOS ≥ 7) and together enrolled 272 patients, 144 in the LPE arm and 128 in the RPE arm. Operation time (MD 0.20, 95% CI - 38.98 to 39.39, P = 0.99), intraoperative blood loss (MD 14.60, 95% CI - 3.39 to 32.58, P = 0.11), postoperative pancreatic fistula (risk ratio [RR] 1.21, 95% CI 0.89-1.64, P = 0.23), postoperative bleeding (RR 0.43, 95% CI 0.06-2.97, P = 0.39), and major complications (RR 1.28, 95% CI 0.54-3.00, P = 0.58) did not differ significantly between groups. Postoperative hospital stay was statistically shorter in the RPE group (MD 1.22, 95% CI 0.29-2.16, P = 0.01); however, this finding should be interpreted cautiously and does not, by itself, establish a clinically meaningful recovery advantage. The available evidence is insufficient to demonstrate a clear overall difference between robotic and laparoscopic pancreatic enucleation in perioperative efficacy or safety. Although postoperative hospital stay was shorter in the RPE group in the pooled analysis, the small observational evidence base and potential residual confounding preclude a firm conclusion that robotic surgery provides a recovery advantage. Larger, well-designed prospective multicentre studies are needed.

items.title: Exercise-containing multimodal prehabilitation on functional outcome of patients with hepatobiliary and pancreatic cancer after surgery: a meta-analysis.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Hepatobiliary and pancreatic (HBP) cancers often require complex surgeries that lead to functional decline and poor quality of life (QoL). Exercise-containing multimodal prehabilitation has gained attention as a potential strategy to enhance perioperative outcomes. This meta-analysis aimed to systematically evaluate the impact of exercise-containing multimodal prehabilitation on functional outcomes in patients with HBP cancers.
METHODS: A systematic search across six electronic databases was undertaken to identify randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and non-randomized studies of interventions (NRSIs) assessing exercise-containing multimodal prehabilitation in adult patients undergoing surgery for HBP cancers. Outcomes included 6-minute walk test (6MWT), QoL, length of stay (LOS), postoperative complications (POCs), and short-term mortality. Random-effects meta-analyses were performed by incorporating potential influence of heterogeneity.
RESULTS: Fifteen studies (8 RCTs and 7 NRSIs) involving 1,643 patients were included. Exercise-containing multimodal prehabilitation significantly improved 6MWT (mean difference [MD]: 30.79 m; 95% CI: 16.98 to 44.59; I² = 72%; p < 0.001) and QoL (standardized mean difference: 0.39; 95% CI: 0.05 to 0.72; I² = 77%; p = 0.02). LOS (MD: -1.10 days; 95% CI: -2.38 to 0.19; p = 0.09), POCs (OR: 0.70; 95% CI: 0.48 to 1.03; p = 0.07), and short-term mortality (OR: 0.80; 95% CI: 0.29 to 2.19; p = 0.67) showed non-significant reductions. The certainty of evidence ranged from moderate (6MWT, QoL) to very low (mortality).
CONCLUSIONS: Exercise-containing multimodal prehabilitation may improve postoperative functional capacity and quality of life in patients undergoing surgery for HBP cancers. However, current evidence for its effects on length of hospital stay, postoperative complications, and mortality remains limited. Further high-quality studies are warranted to confirm these clinical benefits.

items.title: Activity of Fluoro-Substituted 3,5-Di[(E)-Benzylidene]piperidin-4-Ones with N-Arylsulfonyl Appendages Against KRAS-Mutant Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma Cells.
items.abstract: KRAS-mutant pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is characterized by a high mortality that still lacks efficient therapies. Monoketone-based bisarylidene curcuminoid derivatives have shown promising activities against various PDAC models. Based on our previous findings on anticancer-active N-acryloyl-modified piperidin-4-one derivatives, we replaced the reactive acryloyl moiety by a series of N-arylsulfonyl bis-difluoro/trifluoromethylbenzylidene piperidin-4-one derivatives and tested them for antiproliferative activity against KRAS-mutant PDAC cells. Furthermore, apoptosis induction based on caspase-3/7 activation and STAT3 inhibition were investigated for the most promising compound. Notably, the N-tosyl derivative 3a with 4-trifluoromethyl substituents at the benzylidene rings exhibited the highest antiproliferative activities against PDAC cells (IC50 = 0.22-0.26 µM, 48 h). Derivative 3a also strongly induced apoptosis in PDAC cells and suppressed STAT3 activation/phosphorylation, which was supported by molecular docking of this curcuminoid into the SH2 domain of STAT3 and by 3a-STAT3 binding confirmed using CETSA in MiaPaCa-2 cells. These findings identify compound 3a as a promising lead for further preclinical evaluation in KRAS-mutant PDAC models and in other STAT3-dependent cancer types.

items.title: The Cholecystokinin-B Receptor as a Candidate Diagnostic Biomarker and Translational Target for Precision Oncology in Pancreatic Cancer.
items.abstract: Background/Objectives: Identification of cell-surface receptors on cancer tissues that are absent in the corresponding normal tissue provide an opportunity for target-specific diagnostics and drug delivery. The cholecystokinin-B receptor (CCKBR) was initially overlooked as a high-priority biomarker for pancreatic cancer (PDAC) because comparisons were made between cancer and "normal adjacent tissue" from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA). Since PDAC is highly invasive and significantly alters the tumor microenvironment, we now know the adjacent tissue is not normal in PDAC. Methods: A multi-cohort transcriptomic analysis was conducted to evaluate the true expression landscape of CCKBR in human pancreatic tissue. Bulk RNA-sequencing data were harmonized from the Genotype-Tissue Expression (GTEx) repository (N = 328) with true normal pancreas samples and TCGA Pancreatic Adenocarcinoma cohort (N = 178) primary tumors. Confirmation of CCKBR protein expression was performed using a human tissue array. The significance of a single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP, rs1800843) that results in CCKBR mis-splicing was characterized. A biodegradable fluorescent polyplex nanoparticle (NP) was developed to selectively target the CCKBR and was tested using p48-Cre/LSL-KrasG12D (KC) mice. Results: CCKBR transcripts exhibited a profound, binary-like upregulation in malignant tissue compared to normal tissue, achieving statistical significance (p = 10-60). The germline SNP of the CCKBR (rs1800843) was identified in ~40% of patients with confirmed PDAC. Immunoreactivity for the CCKBR protein was absent in normal human pancreas but increased in precancerous PanIN lesions and cancer. A fluorescent labeled CCKBR-targeted NP revealed uptake in the pancreas of KC mice and localized to the PanIN lesions. Conclusions: These data provide new insights into CCKBR, supporting its potential as a diagnostic biomarker and a therapeutic target in precision pancreatic oncology.

items.title: Synergizing Against RAS: The Evolving Landscape of Targeted Combinations in Pancreatic Cancer.
items.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), the most common histological subtype of pancreatic cancer, remains one of the most lethal solid malignancies, with most patients presenting with advanced disease and limited therapeutic options. Activating KRAS mutations are present in over 90% of PDACs and drive tumor initiation, progression, metabolic reprogramming, and immune evasion, making KRAS a central therapeutic target. Advances in drug development have transformed RAS from a historically "undruggable" oncogene into a clinically actionable target through the development of mutation-selective inhibitors, pan-RAS inhibitors, targeted degraders, and RNA-based therapies. The 2026 approval of daraxonrasib by the FDA for metastatic pancreatic cancer marked the first regulatory approval of a RAS-targeted inhibitor in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma and validated RAS blockade as a clinically actionable therapeutic strategy. This review highlights emerging combination strategies designed to maximize the therapeutic potential of RAS inhibition in PDAC. Early clinical studies combining KRAS-targeted therapies with standard chemotherapy have demonstrated encouraging response rates and have led to multiple ongoing phase III trials. As the field moves toward precision oncology, biomarker-driven patient selection, circulating tumor DNA monitoring, and adaptive clinical trial designs will be essential for translating these advances into meaningful survival benefits. Collectively, rational combination strategies represent the next frontier in KRAS-directed therapy and hold the greatest promise for improving outcomes in PDAC.

items.title: Gut microbiota-driven hippuric acid hydrolysis promotes pancreatic tumorigenesis by suppressing NK cell activity.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains one of the most lethal malignancies, characterized by a lack of effective early detection, profoundly immunosuppressive microenvironment, and poor responsiveness to current therapies. Emerging evidence suggests that gut microbiota and their metabolites play important roles in pancreatic tumorigenesis. Glycoproteins shed from pancreatic precancerous lesions may influence the composition of the gut microbiota and their metabolites.
METHODS: We established a pancreatic precancerous lesion mouse model and performed integrated fecal metagenomic sequencing and non-targeted metabolomic profiling to characterize microbiota composition and metabolite alterations. Further we use plasma samples from patients, in vitro cytotoxicity assays and in vivo orthotopic pancreatic tumor models, fecal microbiota transplantation and pancreatic homogenate gavage to assess the effect of microbiota and metabolite alterations. And we conduct RNA sequencing, qPCR, ELISA, flow cytometry, molecular docking, and surface plasmon resonance to further explore its mechanisms.
RESULTS: We identified hippuric acid as a key microbiota-derived metabolite that was significantly reduced during pancreatic tumorigenesis, which was associated with suppressed anti-tumor immunity and enhanced PDAC progression. This reduction was associated with enrichment of microbiota harboring hippurate hydrolase and correlated with poor prognosis in PDAC patients. Mechanistically, hippuric acid activated IL-21R-STAT3-TBX21 signaling axis, promoting the expression of cytotoxic effector molecules, including granzyme B and perforin, thus enhancing NK cell cytotoxicity. Molecular docking and surface plasmon resonance analyses further suggested a direct interaction between hippuric acid and IL-21R.
CONCLUSIONS: Collectively, our study uncovers a previously unrecognized positive feedback regulatory loop involving the PDAC-gut microbiota-hippuric acid-NK cell-PDAC axis and highlights the critical role of gut microbiota and their metabolites in pancreatic tumorigenesis.

items.title: Mucin-1 (MUC1) up-regulates autophagy-related 12 (ATG12) mRNA and protein levels in pancreatic cancer cell lines.
items.abstract: Mucin-1 (MUC1) and Autophagy-related 12 (ATG12) are frequently overexpressed in Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma (PDAC) patients and are correlated with reduced survival time. MUC1 is known for increasing PDAC cell survival through multiple mechanisms, including via the RAS pathway and control of gene transcription. ATG12 is found predominantly within the ATG12-ATG5 covalent complex necessary for the autophagy process required for survival of PDAC cells. Unconjugated ATG12 is known to be tightly regulated due to its pro-apoptotic nature and degraded rapidly downstream of RAS signaling, though effector proteins have not been identified. Mutant KRAS is almost universally mutated in PDAC, therefore our goal was to explore whether MUC1 was an effector of Ras influencing the degradation of ATG12 protein. Here, we report that ATG12 immunoprecipitated with MUC1CT2 in S2-013 cell lines by both LC-MS analysis and western blotting. Unconjugated ATG12 protein levels were significantly elevated in CD11 MUC1+ cell lines as compared to MUC1 knockout cell lines, which implies that MUC1 may regulate ATG12 protein levels. We found that MUC1 significantly up-regulates ATG12 mRNA in both CD11 and S2-013 cell lines. We also found that MUC1 stabilized free ATG12 protein. Collectively, these results identify a previously unknown mechanism by which MUC1 stabilizes ATG12 protein and regulates ATG12 transcription.

items.title: Recent Advancements in Diagnosis and Targeted Therapy of Pancreatic Cancer.
items.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Pancreatic Cancer (PC) is an exceptionally belligerent and lethal malignancy owing to failure in prognosis and limited existing therapies. Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma (PDAC) mostly originates from ductal cells, with a survival rate of less than 5 years. This cancer is predominantly caused by genetic abnormalities in the exocrine pancreas, such as KRAS and p53, which contribute to tumor growth and progression.
OBJECTIVE: Our previously published article on PC taught us that there is an utmost need to identify novel biomarkers for diagnosis and targeted therapy approaches to improve survival rates in patients. Conventional radiotherapy and nanotechnology-based approaches show limited success compared to targeted therapy.
METHODS: A comprehensive literature search was conducted in PubMed, Science Direct, Scopus, Bentham Science, Google Scholar, ACS Journals, and Taylor and Francis journals and Web of Science databases using keywords related to Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma (PDAC), biomarkers, and targeted therapies. Articles published in English over the past two decades were screened, and studies focusing on novel biomarkers and therapeutic strategies were included for this review.
RESULTS: Recent innovations in PDAC treatment include novel biomarkers (genetic markers, proteomic biomarkers, metabolism-related biomarkers, epigenetic markers, liquid biopsy, Pancreatic Cancer Stem Cell (PSCC) biomarkers, circulating biomarkers, and tissue biomarkers) that facilitate early diagnosis and thus minimize mortality rates. The current review highlighted the utmost need for novel targeted approaches (targeting DNA repairing and Microsatellite instability, targeting epigenetic alteration, targeting key Signaling pathways, targeting the stroma, Fibrosis, and extracellular matrix, and drug conjugate inhibitors) that enhance the specificity and efficacy against cancer cells, reduce the injury to healthy tissue, and improve survival rates.
DISCUSSION: Targeted therapy also focuses on the specific molecular characteristics of cancer cells, providing a possible alternative to traditional therapies.
CONCLUSION: To summarize, the shifting landscape of cancer treatment, particularly for PC, requires further study of targeted innovative combination therapies to improve patient survival while addressing the major limitations of traditional treatments. Several such products are in clinical trials, which have benefited patients with new hope suffering from PDAC.

items.title: Liver Metastasis in Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma: Regulatory Mechanisms and Clinical Significance
items.abstract:
Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is a highly aggressive malignancy with a poor prognosis, and liver metastasis is a major contributor to treatment failure and reduced survival. Due to the complex mechanisms underlying tumor progression and metastasis, effective early diagnostic biomarkers and targeted therapeutic strategies remain limited. This study aims to investigate the molecular mechanisms underlying PDAC progression and liver metastasis, identify potential biomarkers for early risk prediction and prognostic assessment, and explore novel therapeutic targets to facilitate precision diagnosis and treatment.

Participants will be required to:

* Provide histopathologically confirmed primary PDAC tissue and liver metastatic tissue, together with the corresponding adjacent non-tumor pancreatic tissue
* Undergo regular follow-up visits for monitoring and data collection.
* Allow access to their medical records for relevant clinical information.

items.title: Targeting lipid metabolism to overcome immunosuppression and enhance immunotherapy or chemotherapy sensitivity in pancreatic cancer: from immunosuppressive mechanisms to therapeutic opportunities.
items.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is characterized by immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME), in which immunosuppression and immune evasion lead to poor response to therapies. Lipid metabolism reprogramming is a central feature of PDAC progression and, depending on the lipid species and context, can promote immunosuppression and immune evasion. Here, we summarize the regulation of lipid metabolism in PDAC and the TME and highlight therapeutic targeting potential. KRAS mutations drive the abnormal activation of key molecules such as SREBP1, FASN, and CD36, promoting de novo fatty acid synthesis, cholesterol metabolism, and the uptake of extracellular lipids. Tumor cells evade immune surveillance by upregulating immune checkpoint molecules and suppressing antigen presentation, thereby impairing both innate and adaptive antitumor immunity. Lipid overload triggers lipid competition and lipotoxicity, induces CD8⁺ T-cell exhaustion and promotes the recruitment of immunosuppressive cells such as M2 macrophages and myeloid-derived suppressor cells. Pancreatic stellate cells and peritumoral adipocytes undergo profound lipid metabolic reprogramming and influence the lipid metabolism of PDAC cells and immune function through mechanisms such as paracrine signaling, thereby further reinforcing the immunosuppressive microenvironment. Lipid metabolism interventions such as targeting fatty acid synthesis, cholesterol metabolism, and lipid peroxidation-driven ferroptosis in combination with chemotherapy and/or immunotherapy have shown promise in preclinical models. Targeting lipid metabolism can reshape the immunosuppressive microenvironment and enhance the sensitivity to PD-1 blockade and gemcitabine, significantly improving antitumor efficacy. In the future, combining spatial metabolomics and single cell lipidomics may reveal the interactions between lipid metabolism and the immune system and explore the mechanisms underlying the lipid metabolic interaction networks among tumor-immune-and stromal cells.

items.title: Long Noncoding RNA LINC00941 Links Oncogenic KRAS Signaling to Aggressiveness, DNA Repair, and Chemoresistance in Pancreatic Cancer.
items.abstract: Oncogenic KRAS mutations are the primary drivers of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), but the noncoding landscape downstream of KRAS remains to be fully elucidated. Here, by integrating PDAC RNA sequencing and exome data from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA), we identified 49 long intergenic noncoding RNAs (lincRNAs) differentially expressed according to KRAS mutation status. Among these, LINC00941 emerged as a primary candidate, as its expression is regulated by KRAS in both loss- and gain-of-function models and is significantly upregulated in PDAC tumors. Analysis of single-cell RNA sequencing and clinical datasets (TCGA/ICGC) revealed that LINC00941 is significantly enriched in PDAC malignant epithelial cells and correlates with poor PDAC patient prognosis. Functional assays demonstrated that LINC00941 knockdown impairs PDAC cell migration and invasion. Notably, LINC00941-depleted cells exhibit delayed DNA repair following irradiation, as shown by the slower resolution of radiation-induced DNA strand breaks, and increased sensitivity to gemcitabine-induced apoptosis. Transcriptomic and RT-qPCR analyses associated the loss of LINC00941 with a significant reduction in key DNA repair and survival-related genes, including BACH1, TOP2A, and BIRC5. These findings suggest that LINC00941 is required to maintain genomic stability and promote survival under therapeutic stress in KRAS-driven cells. In conclusion, our study identifies a novel KRAS/LINC00941 axis that supports a pro-survival and chemoresistant phenotype in PDAC, positioning LINC00941 as a mediator of the DNA damage response and a potential therapeutic target in PDAC.

items.title: Towards precision oncology in pancreatic cancer: Diagnostic and prognostic biomarkers from conventional methods to liquid biopsy and artificial intelligence-based approaches.
items.abstract: Pancreatic cancer (PC) is known as one of the most aggressive and deadly tumors, with pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) predicted to be the second leading cause of cancer death by 2030. Also, due to the lack of specific symptoms and limitations of biomarkers and screening methods for early diagnosis, most patients are diagnosed at advanced stages and with metastatic disease. Therefore, developing new, high-accuracy diagnostic methods for early diagnosis and monitoring of treatment response in patients is very important for providing appropriate treatment options and improving survival rates. In recent years, despite the progress in diagnostic methods such as imaging techniques, tissue biopsy, liquid biopsy (LB), and tumor marker testing, there are many uncertainties about the specificity and sensitivity of these technologies, as well as challenges in their practical use in the clinic. Also, advancements in artificial intelligence (AI) technology in the field of cancer detection have enabled the screening and early diagnosis of PC in high-risk populations by employing AI algorithms with high computational power in conjunction with biomarkers, medical imaging, and pathological tests. In this article, we comprehensively evaluate the potential and diagnostic effectiveness of established tools for PC, alongside emerging and promising approaches, including liquid biopsy and AI-based methods. We examine their applications in early diagnosis, screening, prognostication, and disease monitoring, while also discussing the key characteristics, advantages, and limitations of each approach, as well as the potential benefits of their integration. Finally, we provide clinical recommendations aimed at improving the early detection of this challenging disease.

items.title: New-Onset Diabetes as a Red Flag for Pancreatic Cancer: From Metabolic Clues to Earlier Detection in Primary Care.
items.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is usually diagnosed at an advanced stage and carries a poor prognosis. In a subset of patients, new-onset diabetes may be an early metabolic manifestation preceding the cancer diagnosis, and its recognition in primary care could help identify people at increased risk, although the benefit of using this association for earlier detection remains uncertain. This narrative review examines the clinical and biological relationship between new-onset diabetes and PDAC and evaluates current strategies for risk stratification, including clinical risk scores such as the Enriching New-onset Diabetes for Pancreatic Cancer (ENDPAC) score, circulating biomarkers, polygenic scoring, and machine-learning models, to identify high-risk populations that could benefit from early detection and to assess whether these tools are ready for routine use. PDAC-associated diabetes differs from typical type 2 diabetes: it tends to occur in older individuals, is accompanied by unexplained weight loss, and progresses more rapidly. Risk-prediction scores perform well in their derivation cohorts but discriminate less well on external validation, and candidate biomarkers, alone or in multi-marker panels, show promising but not yet prospectively confirmed discrimination. Models integrating clinical and genetic data also show promising discrimination, yet none has been shown to detect PDAC earlier or to improve survival. New-onset diabetes may therefore be a warning sign of pancreatic cancer, but current evidence does not support screening of all affected patients; clinical features, biomarkers, and genetic information may help identify a higher-risk subgroup, and further studies are needed before these tools enter routine practice.

items.title: Neighborhood Deprivation and Circulating Tumor DNA Provide Distinct Prognostic Signals in Localized Pancreatic Cancer
items.abstract:
Purpose: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is the third leading cause of cancer death in the US. Socioeconomic disadvantage, measured by Area Deprivation Index (ADI), may affect outcomes beyond tumor biology. We evaluate ADI and overall survival (OS) in localized PDAC, accounting for KRAS-mutant circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA).

Methods:

165 patients with localized PDAC were prospectively enrolled (NCT04616131; Oct. 2020–Jan. 2026). ADI was dichotomized at the 50th national percentile. OS was compared by group and jointly with ctDNA using Kaplan-Meier analysis. Multivariable Cox assessed ADI and survival, adjusting for clinical covariates and ctDNA, and tested ADI/ctDNA interactions. C-index/likelihood ratio assessed added discriminatory value. Next-generation sequencing detected KRAS-mutant ctDNA.

Results:

High ADI was associated with shorter OS (26.7 vs 30.5 months, p=0.035; HR 1.79, 95% CI 1.09–2.92, p=0.020). Patients with both high ADI and detectable ctDNA had the poorest survival (9.8 vs 38.3 months, p=0.005). ADI and ctDNA each independently predicted shorter survival without significant interaction; combining both improved model discrimination beyond either alone.

Conclusion:

Greater area deprivation is associated with reduced survival in localized PDAC, independently of clinical and tumor biomarkers. ADI and ctDNA may have additive value for risk stratification, supporting interventions targeting social determinants alongside oncologic care.

items.title: The imPAct of nutritioN on the Outcome of pancrEATic Surgery; Food for Thought.
items.abstract:
Patients with cancer or chronic inflammatory disorders, such as periampullary malignancies or chronic pancreatitis (CP), often experience severe weight loss and a progressive decline in health and functional performance. These changes result from a complex interaction between the disease and the host, affecting multiple physiological factors. However, in daily clinical practice the focus is predominantly placed on treatment of the disorder itself, whereas less attention is given to the physical condition of the patient before treatment commences. Factors such as malnutrition, reduced aerobic fitness, and adverse body composition have all been associated with worse outcomes, including a higher risk of postoperative complications or inability to complete oncological treatment.

The central hypothesis of the investigators is that improving the patient's overall condition before treatment, particularly before major surgery, will enhance treatment tolerance, reduce complications, and improve overall quality of life (QoL). Among the various modifiable factors in the disease-host interaction, nutritional status occupies a central role, directly influencing muscle mass and strength, immune competence, metabolic stability, and recovery capacity.

items.title: Explainable artificial intelligence identifies circulating microRNA candidate biomarkers for liquid biopsy-based pancreatic cancer detection.
items.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Pancreatic cancer (PC) remains a highly lethal malignancy due to asymptomatic progression, late presentation, and lack of reliable minimally invasive liquid biopsy biomarkers for early detection. Circulating microRNAs (c-miRNAs) are promising clinical indicators owing to their stability in body fluids and regulatory influence on oncogenic pathways.
METHODS: This study presents an integrated computational framework combining large-scale serum miRNA expression profiling with differential expression analysis, machine learning (ML), and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI). Five publicly available GEO datasets comprising 1,101 serum samples were analyzed through preprocessing, including normalization, missing-value imputation, and ComBat-based batch correction. A Bayesian stacked ensemble classifier integrating XGBoost, Random Forest, SVC, Naïve Bayes, and k-NN was optimized using SMOTE for class imbalance and constrained weight minimization via SLSQP.
RESULTS: Gene expression analysis identified 148 significantly dysregulated miRNAs (|log2FC| ≥ 2, adj. p < 0.05). The model achieved excellent predictive performance (AUC = 0.97; accuracy = 97.28%; sensitivity = 94%; specificity = 99%). SHAP-based XAI interpretation highlighted 20 miRNAs as the most influential predictors, including hsa-miR-125a-3p, hsa-miR-1290, hsa-miR-614, and hsa-miR-497-5p. Pathway enrichment using DIANA-miRPath and miRDB confirmed their involvement in key oncogenic pathways (MAPK, CDK, TP53).
DISCUSSION: As a retrospective computational study, these findings represent computationally prioritized candidate biomarkers requiring validation in independent external cohorts and experimental approaches before clinical application. The proposed pipeline demonstrates a transparent, reproducible approach for biomarker discovery and validates the clinical promise of circulating miRNAs in minimally invasive liquid biopsy-based early detection of pancreatic cancer.

items.title: OTI1H1-Defined MAGEA3-Directed Immunoreactivity and Survival in Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma: A Single-Center Study.
items.abstract: Background/Objectives: Melanoma-associated antigen A3 (MAGEA3) is a cancer-testis antigen with potential biological and prognostic relevance in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC). This study evaluated the association between OTI1H1-defined MAGEA3-directed immunoreactivity and clinicopathological characteristics and overall survival after pancreatic resection for PDAC. Methods: This retrospective cohort included 76 patients with histologically confirmed PDAC. Patients who died within 30 postoperative days were excluded, and all tumors were retrospectively restaged according to the eighth edition of the AJCC TNM classification. Immunohistochemical staining was assessed using the mouse monoclonal anti-MAGE3 antibody clone OTI1H1 (ab140678, Abcam) by a single experienced pathologist blinded to clinical and outcome data. The percentage of immunoreactive tumor cells was retained as the principal exploratory quantitative measure; the prespecified <10% versus ≥10% classification was evaluated secondarily. Results: Thirty-six of 76 tumors (47.4%) had ≥10% OTI1H1-reactive tumor cells. When staining was modeled continuously, the adjusted HR per 10-percentage-point increase was 0.969 (95% CI 0.898-1.046; p = 0.420). For the secondary binary classification, the adjusted HR for ≥10% versus <10% staining was 0.745 (95% CI 0.417-1.331; p = 0.320). No statistically clear association with overall survival was observed; however, the confidence intervals do not exclude potentially clinically relevant associations in either direction. Conclusions: No statistically clear association between OTI1H1-defined immunoreactivity and overall survival was observed in this cohort. Because OTI1H1 has known cross-reactivity with selected MAGE-A family proteins and no orthogonal molecular validation was performed, these findings should be interpreted as assay-specific and do not establish biological inactivity of MAGEA3 or related MAGE-A proteins.

items.title: Tissue miR-143 and miR-29b Expression as Prognostic Biomarkers in Patients with Resected Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma Receiving Adjuvant Chemotherapy.
items.abstract: Background/Objectives: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) carries one of the worst prognoses among solid tumors, and biomarkers that complement standard pathological variables in patients undergoing resection followed by adjuvant chemotherapy are still lacking. Here, we examined whether tumor expression of 10 selected microRNAs (miRNAs) is associated with recurrence patterns and survival in this clinical setting. Methods: Fifty patients with resected PDAC who received adjuvant chemotherapy at a single institution (2012-2022) were studied retrospectively. Expression of let-7c, miR-10b, miR-27a, miR-29b, miR-31, miR-34a, miR-142, miR-143, miR-17-5p, and miR-200c was measured by quantitative real-time PCR in formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tumor tissue, with adjacent non-tumor pancreatic tissue available for 21 patients. Associations with local recurrence, metastasis, disease-free survival (DFS), and overall survival (OS) were assessed by logistic regression and Cox regression, with miRNA expression dichotomized at the median. Results: Seven miRNAs (let-7c, miR-27a, miR-29b, miR-31, miR-34a, miR-143, miR-200c) were downregulated in tumor tissue and miR-10b was upregulated (all p < 0.05). Higher tumor expression of miR-143 was associated with local recurrence, while higher miR-29b expression was associated with shorter disease-free survival. Adenosquamous histology was independently associated with shorter DFS and OS. Conclusions: Higher tumor expression of miR-143 and miR-29b was associated with local recurrence and shorter disease-free survival, respectively. These exploratory associations require validation in larger independent cohorts.

items.title: Kynureninase Is a Prognostic Biomarker of Poor Survival and Gemcitabine Resistance in Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma.
items.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains one of the deadliest malignancies, largely due to intrinsic or acquired resistance to systemic therapy. In addition to dysregulated glucose metabolism, emerging evidence implicates amino acid metabolism as a key determinant of tumor growth and treatment adaptation. To identify biomarkers associated with chemoresistance, we performed SILAC-based mass spectrometry secretome profiling of gemcitabine-resistant and chemosensitive PDAC cell models, followed by qRT-PCR and immunoblot validation. Functional relevance was assessed by stable shRNA-mediated KYNU knockdown, proliferation assays, and Transwell migration assays. Clinical significance was evaluated by immunohistochemical analysis of KYNU expression in a PDAC tissue microarray (n = 368) and correlation with overall survival. Transcriptomic and pathway enrichment analyses were used to characterize resistance-associated programs. Kynureninase (KYNU), a tryptophan-catabolic enzyme, was upregulated and preferentially secreted by gemcitabine-resistant cells and induced by gemcitabine, interferon-γ, and hypoxia. KYNU knockdown significantly reduced proliferation without affecting migration. Resistant cells displayed higher KYNU expression and a broader therapy-adapted cellular state. In patient samples, high KYNU expression was associated with significantly shorter overall survival (p = 0.0198). These findings identify KYNU as a marker of a therapy-adapted PDAC phenotype and support its potential as a prognostic and treatment-response biomarker.

items.title: Long-Term Outcomes of Anatomical and Biological Borderline Resectable Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma After Gemcitabine/S-1-Based Neoadjuvant Chemoradiotherapy.
items.abstract: Background/Objectives: Oncological outcomes in borderline resectable pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (BR-PDAC) remain unclear. This long-term observational study evaluated these outcomes in patients with BR-PDAC treated with a consistent neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy (CRT) regimen and explored host-related prognostic markers. Methods: We retrospectively analyzed 206 patients with PDAC who received neoadjuvant gemcitabine plus S-1 with concurrent radiotherapy between 2011 and 2022. Biological BR was defined as anatomically resectable disease with an initial carbohydrate antigen 19-9 (CA19-9) level ≥500 U/mL. Anatomical BR was subdivided into portal venous involvement (BR-PV) and arterial involvement (BR-A). Outcomes were compared according to resectability and surgical resection, with resectable (R) patients as a reference. Prognostic factors among resected BR patients were assessed using multivariable Cox regression analysis. Results: The median follow-up was 62.5 months. Resection rates were 85.7%, 83.3%, 69.8%, and 55.6% for R, biological BR, BR-PV, and BR-A, respectively. Although the resection rate of biological BR was similar to that of R, its survival did not differ significantly from that of anatomical BR. Across all BR subtypes, surgical resection was associated with longer overall survival. Among resected patients, the post-CRT neutrophil-lymphocyte-to-monocyte ratio (NL/M), a peripheral blood cell index, was associated with overall survival (hazard ratio 1.020, p = 0.009). Patients with a high post-CRT NL/M had poorer prognosis than those with a low NL/M (p = 0.001). Conclusions: Biological and anatomical BR-PDAC showed no significant difference in long-term survival after neoadjuvant CRT, and surgical resection was associated with longer survival across BR subtypes. Post-CRT NL/M was associated with overall survival after resection and may serve as a potential host-related prognostic marker, although further validation is needed.

items.title: Simple Algorithm for Blood Morphology Analysis (SAMBA): An Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Approach to Identify Peripheral Blood Phenotypes in a Cohort of Patients with Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma (PDAC).
items.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Eosinophils have become important therapeutic targets in several allergic diseases. This study aimed to apply a similar approach-using peripheral blood findings to identify features of type 2 (T2) inflammation-to oncology. We used Simple Algorithm for Blood Morphology Analysis (SAMBA) to describe blood count profiles in a cohort of patients with PDAC independently of relative ratios and propose a potential classification.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: We included 153 treatment-naïve patients with PDAC confirmed by postoperative histopathology. Of these, n = 68 (44.4%) underwent curative surgery, whereas n = 85 (55.6%) received palliative treatment or underwent surgical biopsy only. SAMBA was applied using laboratory reference ranges and overall survival (OS; months) as the analytical context.
RESULTS: The subgroups defined according to laboratory reference ranges did not differ significantly in disease stage, grade, or resection status. Based on correlation analyses, Kaplan-Meier curves, and a classification and regression tree (CART) analysis of OS, we propose four blood count phenotypes: exhausted, lymphopenic, T2-low, and T2-high (median OS: 1.5 months, n = 22; 4.5 months, n = 12; 8.0 months, n = 25; and 10.0 months, n = 94, respectively).
CONCLUSIONS: We propose the following preliminary interpretations of these phenotypes: exhausted, potentially associated with concomitant infection or marked inflammation; lymphopenic, characterized by a low lymphocyte count and potentially reduced antitumor immune activity; eosinopenic (T2-low), characterized by a relatively balanced inflammatory profile but limited T2-associated features; and eosinophilic (T2-high), characterized by no major abnormalities in the other blood count parameters and a more favorable prognosis. SAMBA is a transparent, readily interpretable algorithm that may help standardize and accelerate preliminary research in immuno-oncology.

items.title: A window-of-opportunity trial testing single-dose neoadjuvant hepatic arterial floxuridine and oxaliplatin for patients with localized pancreatic cancer: analysis of safety, feasibility, and interim oncologic outcomes.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Recurrence is common following curative-intent therapy for localized pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), with the liver representing the most frequent site of relapse. Neoadjuvant hepatic artery (HA) chemotherapy improved outcomes in localized colorectal cancer. We evaluated the safety and feasibility of this approach in localized PDAC.
METHODS: This prospective, non-randomized trial treated 20 patients with localized PDAC with a single dose of neoadjuvant HA floxuridine (325 mg/m2) and oxaliplatin (37.5 mg/m2) one week before surgical resection. Primary endpoints were 30-day safety and feasibility. Secondary endpoints include three-year disease-free (DFS), liver metastasis-free (LMFS), and overall survival (OS).
RESULTS: HA chemotherapy was successfully delivered in 20 of 21 patients (95.2%). While 14 patients (70%) experienced at least one adverse event within the safety period, only two were possibly related to treatment, including grade 1 and grade 2 transaminitis events that resolved without intervention. No serious adverse events were attributed to treatment. At a median follow up of 13.8 months, 16 patients remain alive (median OS not reached). Seven developed recurrence (median DFS 20.5 months), including four with liver metastases (median LMFS 20.5 months).
CONCLUSIONS: Single-dose neoadjuvant HA chemotherapy is safe and feasible in localized PDAC. Long-term follow-up is ongoing.

items.title: Impact of Clonal Hematopoiesis on Outcomes in Metastatic Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma: Analysis From the PASS-01 Trial.
items.abstract:
PURPOSE: Clonal hematopoiesis (CH) is increasingly recognized as a proinflammatory driver of adverse outcomes in solid tumors. Tumor-infiltrating immune cells with CH (TI-CH) actively promote tumor growth and those harboring TI-CH experience significantly worse survival. We investigated the prevalence and impact of CH on outcomes in patients with treatment-naïve metastatic pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC).
METHODS: Peripheral blood from 125 patients with metastatic PDAC enrolled in the PASS-01 trial (ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT04469556) was evaluated. CH was defined as the presence of pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants with a variant allele frequency (VAF) of ≥1% in a 23 gene panel. Survival was estimated using the Kaplan-Meier method and compared using the log-rank test. Hazard ratios (HRs) were estimated using multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression.
RESULTS: CH was detected in 36.8% (46 of 125) of patients, and DNMT3A (60.9%) and TET2 (17.4%) were the most frequently mutated genes. There was no significant difference in progression-free survival (PFS; median, 4.9 v 5.2 months; HR, 1.01 [95% CI, 0.68 to 1.49]; P = .95) and overall survival (OS; median, 9.4 v 9.6 months; HR, 0.99 [95% CI, 0.63 to 1.53]; P = .95) between CH-positive and CH-negative patients, respectively. Among patients with basal-like subtype (n = 23), the presence of CH was associated with a numerically shorter PFS (median, 2.4 v 4.7 months; HR, 2.50 [95% CI, 0.93 to 6.84]; P = .06) and OS (median, 6.2 v 10.2 months; HR, 1.37 [95% CI, 0.51 to 3.69]; P = .52). In contrast, classical subtype showed no significant differences in survival outcomes by CH.
CONCLUSION: CH is prevalent in metastatic PDAC but not independently prognostic. Further examination of CH in basal subtype tumors and the role of TI-CH in PDAC is needed.

items.title: Radical antegrade modular pancreatosplenectomy versus conventional distal pancreatosplenectomy for left-sided pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma: a multicenter propensity score-matched analysis.
items.abstract:
PURPOSE: This study was performed to evaluate the postoperative and long-term oncologic outcomes of radical antegrade modular pancreatosplenectomy (RAMPS) relative to conventional distal pancreatosplenectomy (cDPS) in patients with left-sided pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC).
METHODS: Between 2005 and 2017, 316 patients with left-sided PDAC who underwent curative-intent distal pancreatectomy at four tertiary referral centers were retrospectively analyzed. Propensity score matching was performed at a 1:2 ratio based on age, sex, tumor differentiation, and T and N stage.
RESULTS: Among 316 patients, 236 underwent RAMPS and 80 underwent cDPS. After propensity score matching, 210 patients with well-balanced baseline characteristics were included (RAMPS, 139; cDPS, 71). The RAMPS group demonstrated a significantly higher R0 resection rate (99.3% vs. 88.6%, P = 0.007) and a greater number of harvested lymph nodes (16.3 ± 11.2 vs. 10.3 ± 7.1, P < 0.001) than the cDPS group. The overall survival (OS) (median, 26 months vs. 31 months; P = 0.963) and disease-free survival (DFS) (median, 11 months vs. 9 months; P = 0.148) did not differ between the groups. In an exploratory analysis of node-negative patients, RAMPS showed a favorable trend toward improved DFS; however, the operative method was not an independent prognostic factor for either DFS or OS in multivariate analysis. Tumor-related factors, rather than the operative method, were independently associated with long-term outcomes.
CONCLUSION: Despite superior margin clearance and lymph node retrieval, RAMPS did not improve long-term survival compared with cDPS, even in node-negative disease, indicating that outcomes in left-sided PDAC are driven more by tumor biology than by the surgical approach.
