items.title: Prognostic utility of the sphingolipid metabolic pathway in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Sphingolipid metabolism regulates physiologic responses through the sphingomyelin-ceramide-sphingosine-1-phosphate axis. Acid sphingomyelinase has previously been associated with improved outcomes in pancreatic cancer (pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma). In this study, we evaluate acid sphingomyelinase in the context of additional key enzymes in the sphingolipid metabolic pathway in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.
METHODS: An institutional cohort of surgery-first patients (n = 23) and a cohort from the Human Protein Atlas (N = 171) were utilized to examine overall and recurrence-free survival based on key enzyme expression levels including acid sphingomyelinase, the neutral sphingomyelinases (1/2), the downstream acid ceramidase (N-acylsphingosine amidohydrolase 1), and sphingosine kinases (1/2).
RESULTS: In the institutional cohort, 30% of patients had high acid sphingomyelinase expression, 74% had high neutral sphingomyelinase 1 expression, and 22% had high neutral sphingomyelinase 2 expression. There was improved overall survival associated with higher expression of neutral sphingomyelinase 1 (median overall survival, 23.0 vs 15.6 months; P = .0003), and sphingosine kinase 2 (median overall survival, not reached vs 18.9 months; P = .002), and worsened overall survival associated with high sphingosine kinase 1 expression (median overall survival, 19.6 months versus not reached). Acid sphingomyelinase expression was associated with improved recurrence-free survival (23.6 months versus 16.0 months, P = .033) and no cases of local-only recurrence (0% vs 28.6%).
CONCLUSION: Sphingolipid metabolism, particularly high levels of acid sphingomyelinase expression, appears to have prognostic value in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma. Future work should focus on how these findings can be leveraged to improve outcomes in pancreatic cancer.

items.title: ECHS1 K115 succinylation inhibits fatty acid β-oxidation in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.
items.abstract: Metabolic reprogramming is a hallmark of cancer and involves alterations in glucose metabolism. Increasing evidence shows that acylation modifications mediated by metabolic intermediates play vital roles in cancer progression. Toward understanding the lysine succinylation (Ksu) that regulate pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) development, we conduct a comprehensive succinylproteome study on a prospectively collected PDAC cohort. Succinylome integration identifies a range of dysregulated Ksu sites closely associated with metabolic perturbations. Moreover, cross-talk analysis of Ksu and lysine lactylation (Kla) reveals the functional roles of Ksu in proteins specifically related to the fatty acid β-oxidation (FAO), among which, the succinylation at lysine 115 (K115su) of short-chain enoyl-CoA hydratase 1 (ECHS1) is downregulated in pancreatic cancer. It is further verified that K115su reduces the conversion of ECHS1 for its substrate, thereby inhibiting FAO metabolism. Therefore, our study delineates multiple cancer-specific Ksu sites and unravels the significance of ECHS1 K115su in PDAC progression.

items.title: Implementation of a rapid onsite molecular adequacy protocol for endoscopic ultrasound-guided sampling of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.
items.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Current clinical practice guidelines recommend molecular profiling for patients with pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC). However, endoscopic ultrasound-guided small specimens are often insufficient for next-generation sequencing (NGS). In this study, the impact of a standardized protocol designed to optimize tissue acquisition for NGS was evaluated.
METHODS: Quality assurance data from patients with suspected PDAC who underwent endoscopic ultrasound-guided tissue acquisition for NGS was retrospectively analyzed. A standardized workflow incorporating rapid onsite evaluation using predefined adequacy criteria, dedicated tissue procurement for cell block preparation, multidisciplinary communication, and prospective monitoring of molecular outcomes were evaluated using a successful NGS result as the primary endpoint.
RESULTS: Of the 61 patients with confirmed PDAC by cytology, 49 specimens (80.3%) were deemed adequate for NGS during rapid onsite evaluation. Forty-one specimens with a median tumor fraction of 30% underwent NGS. Median DNA and RNA yields were 20.8 ng/µL and 19.7 ng/µL, respectively. DNA-based NGS was successful in 39 cases (95.1%), whereas RNA-based fusion analysis succeeded in 22 cases (53.7%). Median turnaround time from specimen receipt to NGS reporting was 10 business days.
CONCLUSIONS: A standardized molecular adequacy protocol achieved high DNA sequencing success but did not substantially improve overall specimen adequacy compared with prior institutional experience. Intrinsic biologic features of PDAC, including low tumor cellularity and abundant desmoplastic stroma and nonneoplastic elements remain the principal barriers to molecular profiling. Future efforts that focus on improving tumor enrichment and optimizing RNA preservation may expand precision oncology access to patients with PDAC.

items.title: Decoding lipid metabolic reprogramming in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma: from tumor-microenvironment crosstalk to therapeutic resistance.
items.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is characterized by a nutrient-poor, hypoxic, and highly desmoplastic microenvironment that imposes substantial metabolic stress on malignant cells. Under these unfavorable conditions, lipid metabolism reprogramming provides cancer cells with the flexibility needed to maintain growth and survive therapeutic stress. Recent advances have uncovered new links between lipid metabolic reprogramming, the tumor microenvironment, and therapeutic resistance in PDAC, highlighting the need for an updated synthesis of this rapidly evolving field. In this review, we focus on the major tumor-intrinsic alterations in fatty acid and cholesterol-mevalonate metabolism, including changes in lipid synthesis, uptake, desaturation, storage, and oxidative utilization. These processes support membrane homeostasis, oncogenic signaling, and redox control, thereby linking lipid handling directly to tumor progression and treatment adaptation. We further review how these pathways are reshaped by the tumor microenvironment, where cancer-associated fibroblasts, immune cells, adipocytes, and neural-associated cells influence lipid availability, trafficking, and signaling. These reciprocal interactions can shape stromal plasticity, immune suppression, invasion, metastasis, and treatment response. We also evaluate current strategies targeting lipid metabolism and discuss why their clinical translation remains limited by metabolic compensation, tumor heterogeneity, drug specificity, and systemic toxicity. Overall, the available evidence suggests that lipid metabolism in PDAC is better understood as a dynamic, interconnected adaptive network rather than a set of isolated metabolic pathways. This perspective supports biomarker-guided combination strategies that target context-dependent lipid dependencies and treatment-induced metabolic adaptation, rather than relying on inhibition of a single pathway.

items.title: Does Stent Externalization Matter in Robotic Pancreaticoduodenectomy? A Risk-Stratified Comparison of Internal and External Pancreatic Stenting.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Postoperative pancreatic fistula (POPF) remains a significant source of morbidity following pancreaticoduodenectomy (PD), and whether internal or external stenting better mitigates POPF after robotic PD (RPD) remains unclear.
METHODS: A retrospective review was conducted of patients who underwent RPD with internalized or externalized pancreatic duct stents at a single academic institution (2020-2026). POPF was graded by ISGPS criteria, with risk stratified by Fistula Risk Score (FRS) and Alternative FRS (A-FRS). Ninety-day outcomes were recorded.
RESULTS: Of 182 patients, 83 (45.6%) received an externalized stent. Age, sex, BMI, and PDAC proportion were similar between internal and external stent groups, as was fistula risk (74.7% vs. 71.1% intermediate/high risk) (all p > 0.05). Overall POPF rate was nearly identical (18.2% vs. 18.1%; p = 0.985), with most fistulas (73.5%) being biochemical leaks and no Grade C fistulas. Among low/intermediate A-FRS patients, clinically-relevant POPF rates were comparable (2.6% vs. 2.9%; p = 0.994). In high A-FRS patients, external stenting was associated with significantly fewer clinically-relevant POPFs (0.0% vs. 21.7%) and more biochemical leaks (35.7% vs. 8.7%, p = 0.04). External stenting did not increase length of stay or readmission.
CONCLUSIONS: In high fistula-risk RPD patients, external stenting was associated with fewer clinically-relevant POPFs, suggesting externalization may prevent progression to clinically-relevant POPF.

items.title: The ABHD10-ACSL4 axis promotes pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma growth via suppressing ferroptosis.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is a highly aggressive malignancy with poor prognosis and limited treatment options. Ferroptosis has emerged as a potential therapeutic vulnerability in PDAC, but the upstream mechanisms regulating this process remain unclear. This study aimed to identify compounds with therapeutic potential against PDAC, determine their molecular targets, and elucidate how alpha/beta hydrolase domain-containing protein 10 (ABHD10) regulates tumor growth.
METHODS: A high-throughput compound screen against PDAC cell proliferation was performed, followed by limited proteolysis-mass spectrometry to identify the molecular target of halofuginone (HF). Target engagement was validated by surface plasmon resonance, cellular thermal shift assay, and drug affinity responsive target stability assay. Gain- and loss-of-function studies were conducted in PDAC cell lines and xenograft mouse models. Protein interaction, palmitoylation, and ferroptosis-related changes were evaluated using co-immunoprecipitation, acyl-biotinyl exchange, Click-iT labeling, transmission electron microscopy, and biochemical assays. Statistical analyses included Student's t tests and one-way or two-way analysis of variance, as appropriate.
RESULTS: HF significantly suppressed PDAC growth in vitro and in vivo. ABHD10 was identified as a direct binding target of HF and was upregulated in pancreatic cancer tissues and cell lines. Functional studies showed that ABHD10 promoted cell proliferation, survival, and tumor progression. Mechanistically, ABHD10 interacted with acyl-CoA synthetase long-chain family member 4 (ACSL4) and depalmitoylated it at cysteine 157, thereby suppressing ferroptosis. HF treatment or ABHD10 depletion increased ACSL4 palmitoylation, enhanced lipid peroxidation, disrupted redox homeostasis, and induced ferroptotic changes. Depletion of ACSL4 partially reversed these effects.
CONCLUSION: The ABHD10-ACSL4 axis promotes PDAC growth by suppressing ferroptosis. Targeting this pathway may represent a promising therapeutic strategy for PDAC.

items.title: Ecosystem Determinants of Therapeutic Resistance in Pancreatic Cancer: Implications for Precision Oncology.
items.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains highly lethal despite advances in systemic and biomarker-directed therapy. Treatment resistance reflects not only tumor genotype but also desmoplasia, vascular dysfunction, immune suppression, metabolic adaptation, and evolutionary plasticity. This review integrates signaling dependency, ecosystem architecture, and adaptive evolution into an ecosystem-adaptive framework to explain therapeutic failure in PDAC and proposes four candidate ecosystem states: desmoplastic exclusion, myeloid dominance, hypoxic-metabolic adaptation, and immune-interface organization. These dynamic states may influence therapeutic exposure and resistance beyond conventional molecular classification. Prospective validation could support biomarker development, therapeutic stratification, rational treatment combinations, and treatment sequencing in pancreatic cancer.

items.title: RNA sequencing and proteomic analysis of diagnostic biopsies from colorectal and pancreatic cancer.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Colorectal cancer (CRC) and pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) are two of the most frequently occurring and lethal cancers. Although numerous studies have investigated their transcriptional, molecular, and immunological landscapes, our current understanding remains incomplete. Both cancers pose major clinical challenges, and better understanding of their molecular and immunological profiles is needed to improve patient outcomes.
METHODS: We conducted total RNA sequencing and liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry-based proteomic profiling of 29 diagnostic biopsies from both primary tumors and metastatic sites in 16 CRC and 11 PDAC patients. Due to a lack of tissue, PDAC primary tumors were only analyzed by proteomics. Data analysis involved RNA-to-protein correlation analysis, multidimensional scaling, sample-to-sample Pearson correlations visualized as heatmaps with unsupervised clustering, differential expression analysis, gene ontology (GO) enrichment analysis, and immune cell deconvolution using CIBERSORTx.
RESULTS: Analyzing all available biopsies, RNA sequencing identified 46,492 expressed transcripts and proteomic analysis detected 6973 proteins, with 5563 genes common to both datasets. The mean absolute RNA-to-protein Spearman correlation was 0.241. In CRC, exploratory differential expression analysis identified 5 transcripts and 99 proteins differing between metastases and primary tumors. In PDAC, metastasis-to-primary tumor comparison was limited to proteomics and identified 305 differentially expressed proteins. In unsupervised clustering based on sample-to-sample correlation, CRC and PDAC biopsies formed two separate clusters. GO enrichment analysis demonstrated distinct patterns of up- and downregulation across molecular functions, cellular components, and biological processes in metastases compared with primary tumors. Inferred immune cell fractions indicated high levels of CD4 T memory resting cells and M0 macrophages.
CONCLUSIONS: This exploratory study supports the feasibility of combined RNA sequencing and proteomic profiling from limited FFPE diagnostic biopsies and highlights proteomics as an important complement to transcriptomics. These findings enhance our understanding of biological and immunological heterogeneity and require further validation in larger independent cohorts for future development of prognostic markers and novel immunotherapeutic strategies.

items.title: A Modified Blumgart Pancreaticojejunostomy in Laparoscopic Pancreaticoduodenectomy: A Retrospective Study.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Laparoscopic pancreaticoduodenectomy (LPD) is increasingly performed, but clinically relevant postoperative pancreatic fistula (CR-POPF) remains a major complication. This study evaluated a modified Blumgart pancreaticojejunostomy (PJ) technique in LPD.
METHODS: This retrospective study included 217 consecutive patients who underwent LPD between January 2021 and December 2025. 102 in the modified Blumgart group and 115 in the conventional Blumgart group. 1:1 propensity score matching (PSM) was performed using 12 covariates based on the Fistula Risk Score model. The primary outcome was CR-POPF. Univariate and multivariate logistic regression identified independent risk factors, and exploratory subgroup analyses were conducted.
RESULTS: After PSM, 78 patients remained in each group. In the entire cohort, the modified group had a significantly lower CR-POPF rate (6.9% vs. 17.4%, p = 0.019) and fewer abdominal infections (5.9% vs. 15.7%, p = 0.022). After PSM, CR-POPF remained lower in the modified group (7.7% vs. 17.9%, p = 0.055), and abdominal infection remained significantly reduced (6.4% vs. 16.7%, p = 0.045). Multivariate analysis identified PDAC pathology (OR = 0.233, p = 0.022) and modified anastomosis (OR = 0.383, p = 0.041) as independent protective factors in the entire cohort. Subgroup analysis revealed that the protective effect was shown in patients with a main pancreatic duct > 3 mm (OR = 0.176, p = 0.008; PSM cohort: OR = 0.169, p = 0.027; p for interaction = 0.070 and 0.111, respectively).
CONCLUSIONS: The modified Blumgart PJ is safe and effective in LPD, reducing CR-POPF and abdominal infection. Its protective effect is shown in patients with a main pancreatic duct > 3 mm.

items.title: Theranostic lipid nanocarriers for precision diagnosis and targeted therapy in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.
items.abstract: Pancreatic cancer is among the most prevalent ones, and its diagnosis typically occurs in the latter stages. Traditional chemotherapy is usually limited by low tumour penetration, systemic toxicity, and drug resistance. The new method of drug delivery utilizing nanotechnology has proven an effective strategy for addressing these shortcomings by improving drug solubility, efficacy, targeted distribution, and pharmacokinetic properties. This review addresses the genesis of pancreatic cancer, detection, current therapy, and all aspects discussed in carrier-based drug delivery modalities. A specific focus is placed on different types of lipid-based nanocarriers and nanoemulsions, the peculiarities of their formulation, and experimental results. These nanocarriers have been critically reviewed with respect to clinical benefits, therapeutic potential, and translational progress. Besides, new patent regulatory issues regarding nanomedicines for pancreatic cancer. Although there were good clinical outcomes, issues of standardization and control need to be addressed by the solution before nanocarrier-based therapies can be applied in the clinic. Future advancements in personalized nanomedicine, biomarker-guided targeting, and AI-assisted formulation strategies may further enhance the therapeutic efficacy and diagnostic precision of lipid-based nanocarriers in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC). In addition, the integration of nanocarrier systems with combination immunotherapy and precision medicine approaches holds significant promise for improving clinical translation and patient-specific treatment outcomes.

items.title: Feasibility study of habitat imaging based on DCE-MRI combined with clinical and imaging features for predicting lymph node metastasis in patients with pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND: To investigate the feasibility of preoperative prediction of lymph node metastasis in patients with pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) using habitat imaging (HI) based on dynamic contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (DCE-MRI) combined with clinical and imaging features.
METHODS: A retrospective analysis was conducted on 62 patients with pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, including 22 patients in the lymph node metastasis (LNM)-positive group and 40 patients in the LNM-negative group. The U-test or t-test was used to compare differences in clinical features, imaging features and interpretable imaging phenotypes between the two groups. Spearman correlation analysis was performed, and Partial Least Squares Regression (PLS) was selected as the primary modeling method. Clinical model, habitat model and combined model were established to predict lymph node metastasis. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves based on five-fold cross-validation were used to evaluate the diagnostic performance of the models.
RESULTS: CA19-9, Spatial Separation, Spatial Calinski-Harabasz, Kinetic Separation, Kinetic Davies-Bouldin and Kinetic Silhouette Coefficient showed statistically significant differences between the two groups (all P < 0.05). Spatial Separation, Kinetic Separation, Kinetic Davies-Bouldin Index, Kinetic Silhouette Coefficient and CA19-9 levels were correlated with lymph node metastasis in PDAC (r = - 0.326, - 0.326, - 0.27, 0.302, and 0.3, respectively; all P < 0.05). ROC curve analysis indicated that the combined model demonstrated significantly improved predictive performance compared with the clinical model (P = 0.042), whereas no statistically significant differences were observed between the combined and habitat models (P = 0.121) or between the habitat and clinical models (P = 0.243).
CONCLUSIONS: Habitat imaging based on DCE-MRI was effective in predicting lymph node metastasis in PDAC, and integrating habitat and clinical information may improve model discrimination ability.

items.title: Association of Psychological Distress With Clinical Outcomes in Patients With Digestive System Cancers
items.abstract:
This prospective observational cohort study aims to investigate the association between psychological distress and clinical outcomes in patients with digestive system cancers, including pancreatic, gastric, and colorectal cancers.

Approximately 100 adult patients who are scheduled to receive first-line systemic anticancer therapy will be enrolled at Xuanwu Hospital, Capital Medical University. Psychological distress will be assessed using the Distress Thermometer (DT), Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS), and 12-item General Health Questionnaire (GHQ-12).

Participants will undergo baseline assessments and follow-up evaluations every three months for up to three years. Clinical information, psychological distress scores, laboratory findings, imaging results, and quality-of-life data will be collected.

The primary outcome is progression-free survival (PFS). Secondary outcomes include overall survival (OS), objective response rate (ORR), and quality of life. The study will evaluate whether psychological distress is associated with cancer prognosis after adjusting for potential confounding factors, including cancer stage, treatment regimen, and nutritional status.

As an observational study, no experimental treatment will be assigned, and all participants will receive standard anticancer treatment according to routine clinical practice.

items.title: Novel Pathogenic Roles and Mechanisms of Fibrinogen in Pancreatic Cancer
items.abstract:
The dismal prognosis associated with pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is attributed to the aggressive
nature of these tumors and the lack of effective screening or treatment strategies. PDAC is especially problematic
for the U.S. Veterans population, which has a higher PDAC prevalence than the general population. Studies
have shown that patients with PDAC have a high rate of venous thromboembolism (VTE), which is also an
important cancer-associated factor in the Veteran population. Critically, patients with VTE are more likely to have
an advanced stage of cancer and worse prognosis than patients without VTE. Fibrinogen is primarily considered
in the context of hemostasis; however, it is also important for other processes such as cell-cell interaction,
inflammation, and tumorigenesis. Although fibrinogen levels are elevated in cancer patient plasma and cancer
tissues, the mechanistic roles for fibrinogen in the pathogenesis of any cancer, including PDAC, are largely
unknown. We have performed extensive preliminary studies to show functional roles of fibrinogen in PDAC. For
the current project, we hypothesize that increased fibrinogen expression in the basal subtype of PDAC plays an
important role in cancer progression through the AKT/STAT3 signaling axis, thereby promoting EMT/metastasis,
chemoresistance and anti-apoptosis in cancer cells. We propose that a novel therapy (A2 protein) targeting
fibrinogen in combination with the first-line chemotherapeutic drug regimen (FOLFIRINOX) could be beneficial
primarily for PDAC patients with basal subtype tumors. Two specific aims are proposed: 1). Determine the
functions and molecular mechanisms of tumor-derived fibrinogen in the pathogenesis of the basal subtype of
PDAC in vitro and in vivo. 2). Determine the therapeutic efficacy of the novel combination of chemotherapy with
A2 protein targeting fibrinogen in the basal subtype of PDAC in PDX mouse models.
The proposed project is highly relevant to U.S. veterans due to their increased risk for PDAC. With the in depth
research on roles of tumor-derived and systemic fibrinogen on PDAC progression, and effective targeting
strategy, we expect this project to offer a new, groundbreaking paradigm for VA patient care, and bring a novel
treatment option for basal subtype of PDAC patients. Results obtained from the current project will be ready to
implement into clinical trials.

items.title: Bioabsorbable spacer-assisted high-dose proton beam therapy for unresectable locally advanced pancreatic cancer of the body or tail: a feasibility and safety study.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: Anatomical proximity to gastrointestinal (GI) organs can preclude dose-escalated irradiation for locally advanced pancreatic cancer (LAPC). We evaluated the safety and feasibility of bioabsorbable spacer-assisted high-dose proton beam therapy (PBT) for unresectable LAPC of the pancreatic body or tail.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: This exploratory retrospective analysis used retrospectively reviewed perioperative data and retrospectively or prospectively collected PBT data. Fourteen patients with presumed nonmetastatic LAPC underwent placement of a bioabsorbable polyglycolic acid (PGA) spacer. Thirteen received definitive PBT at 67.5 or 75 Gy (relative biological effectiveness [RBE]) in 25 fractions. The composite primary safety endpoint was the occurrence of a Clavien-Dindo grade ≥III surgical complication or a CTCAE grade ≥3 adverse event related to definitive PBT or concurrent chemotherapy.
RESULTS: Spacer placement achieved ≥10 mm tumor-GI separation in all 14 patients; 13 completed definitive PBT. No Clavien-Dindo grade ≥III surgical complication occurred. Four of 13 definitive-PBT patients (30.8%) experienced at least one qualifying safety event: one experienced grade 3 nausea and three other patients experienced grade 3 leukopenia/neutropenia. No grade ≥3 structural GI injury was observed. Median follow-up was 19.3 months. Median overall and progression-free survival were 24.8 and 11.8 months, respectively; 1- and 2-year local control rates were 81.5% and 38.2%.
CONCLUSION: Bioabsorbable spacer-assisted high-dose PBT was technically feasible in this selected cohort. However, this small, uncontrolled study cannot establish a low risk of uncommon or late adverse events or support conclusions regarding comparative safety or efficacy.

items.title: Tumo​r-associated macrophages in ovarian, prostate, thyroid and pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors: molecular crosstalk and therapeutic perspectives.
items.abstract: Tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) are key regulators of the tumor microenvironment and play dual roles in endocrine cancer progression by exhibiting remarkable functional plasticity beyond the conventional M1/M2 paradigm. Their interactions with tumor cells influence immune evasion, angiogenesis, metastasis, and therapeutic resistance through complex signaling networks and extracellular vesicle-mediated communication. This review summarizes the current understanding of TAM biology across some key endocrine and hormone-dependent cancers, including ovarian, prostate, thyroid, and pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors, highlighting their prognostic significance and molecular mechanisms. We further discuss emerging TAM-targeted therapeutic strategies, including macrophage depletion, immune checkpoint modulation, macrophage reprogramming, and nanoparticle-based approaches. Finally, we outline the challenges associated with clinical translation and emphasize the potential of single-cell and multi-omics technologies to enable precision macrophage-targeted therapies for endocrine cancers, including a summary of recent developments in the field of precision mapping of TAMs.

items.title: LncRNA signatures associated with exhausted CD8⁺T cells for assessing the immune microenvironment and drug sensitivity in pancreatic adenocarcinoma.
items.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Pancreatic adenocarcinoma (PAAD) is an aggressive malignancy with generally poor prognosis characterized by significant immune evasion driven primarily by its immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME). A central mechanism underlying this evasion is T cell exhaustion (Tex), particularly in CD8⁺T cells, which limits effective anti-tumor immune responses. This study aimed to identify exhausted CD8⁺T cell-related long non-coding RNAs (CD8TexRLs) and evaluate their clinical relevance, with a focus on constructing a prognostic model, assessing immune microenvironment features, and identifying functionally important lncRNA candidates.
BASIC METHODS: To elucidate underlying mechanisms and therapeutic implications, comprehensive analyses covering pathway enrichment, TMB, immune landscape profiling, and drug response prediction were conducted. PAAD samples were further stratified into distinct molecular subtypes using ConsensusClusterPlus. Tumor clonogenic assays and subcutaneous tumor modeling were employed to investigate the impact of AC053503.1 overexpression and knockdown in CD8⁺T cell models on PAAD cell proliferation. Immunohistochemistry revealed that AC053503.1 knockdown in CD8⁺T cells significantly enhanced the tumor proliferation rate.
MAIN RESULTS: Seven signature CD8TexRLs-AL162424.1, MIR3142HG, LINC02004, AC053503.1, FLRT1, AC068580.2, and AP005233.2-were identified and integrated into a prognostic model that divided patients into high- and low-risk groups. High-risk individuals displayed pronounced enrichment of B-cell receptor signaling and cytosolic DNA-sensing pathways, together with increased TMB and an altered immune landscape. The model also identified differences in immune features and predicted drug sensitivity between risk groups. Stratification into molecular subtypes further demonstrated distinct immune profiles and predicted therapeutic sensitivities. Functional validation revealed that lncRNA AC053503.1 acts as a tumor suppressor in PAAD, with its knockdown promoting tumor proliferation.
CONCLUSIONS: In summary, our research delineates the complex role of exhausted CD8⁺T cells within the PAAD tumor microenvironment and establishes CD8TexRLs as promising biomarkers for predicting both immunotherapy responses and patient survival. Particularly, functional characterization confirmed lncRNA AC053503.1 as a suppressor of PAAD proliferation, revealing new avenues for targeted therapeutic development.

items.title: Periodontitis and pancreatic cancer: the oral-gut microbial axis, pathogenic mechanisms, and potential therapeutic implications.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Pancreatic cancer is a highly aggressive malignancy with a poor prognosis. Epidemiological studies have suggested a possible association between periodontitis and pancreatic cancer, while microbiome studies have reported alterations in the oral, gut, and pancreatic microbiota.
OBJECTIVE: This review examines the evidence linking periodontitis to pancreatic cancer, with particular attention to microbial interactions along the proposed oral-gut microbial axis.
DESIGN: This narrative review synthesizes current epidemiological, microbiome, and experimental evidence relevant to the potential association between periodontitis and pancreatic cancer.
RESLUTS: Experimental studies suggest that periodontitis-associated microorganisms, including Porphyromonas gingivalis and Fusobacterium nucleatum, or their products, may reach the pancreas via digestive or circulatory routes. These microorganisms may influence the development and progression of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma through chronic inflammation, immune evasion, virulence factors, microbial metabolites, and the activation of oncogenic signaling pathways. Specific oral and gut microbial features have been investigated as candidate biomarkers. Periodontal treatment, dietary modification, and probiotics have also been studied for their effects on microbial composition and inflammation-related pathways potentially relevant to pancreatic cancer. The clinical relevance of these candidate biomarkers remains to be established, and microbial alterations may either contribute to pancreatic cancer or occur as a consequence of the disease.
CONCLUSIONS: Current evidence supports a possible link between periodontitis and pancreatic cancer, although the role of microbiota in this relationship remains under investigation.

items.title: Food Environment, Food Access, and Disparities in Pancreatic Cancer Outcomes: A Narrative Review of Evidence Gaps and Future Directions.
items.abstract: Pancreatic cancer has among the poorest survival of any malignancy, with substantial disparities in outcomes. Nutritional status is associated with treatment tolerance, postoperative complications, and survival in pancreatic cancer, while dietary factors have also been associated with pancreatic cancer risk. The food environment, including access to and the relative availability of healthy and unhealthy food retailers, represents a potentially modifiable structural determinant of health. In this narrative review, we summarize evidence on nutrition and pancreatic cancer and on food environment and cancer outcomes. Few studies have examined food environment in pancreatic cancer, and findings are inconsistent. A large U.S. study using a composite food environment measure found associations with later-stage presentation and modestly worse survival, and a county-level analysis reported higher pancreatic cancer mortality in food swamps. Studies examining food desert residence, however, have not demonstrated associations with pancreatic cancer incidence or survival. Multi-cancer studies, including pancreatic cancer, report associations between poor food environments and cancer outcomes but generally do not report pancreas-specific results. Current evidence linking food environment to pancreatic cancer outcomes is limited and extrapolated from other cancers and chronic conditions, comes entirely from the United States, and relies on area-level exposure measures. We describe community interventions to improve food access, none yet evaluated for cancer outcomes, and propose a research agenda to address these gaps.

items.title: Yellow, Red, and Black Lepidium meyenii Preparations Differentially Modulate Doxorubicin Response and Lipid Metabolism-Related Changes in Pancreatic Cancer Cells.
items.abstract: Pancreatic cancer is characterized by cellular heterogeneity, contributing to variable responses to anticancer treatment. Natural products may modify these responses in a context-dependent manner. We investigated whether three Lepidium meyenii Walp. (Brassicaceae; maca) preparations, marked as yellow (MY), red (MR), and black (MB), differentially modify pancreatic cancer cell responses to doxorubicin (DOX). BxPC-3, MIA PaCa-2, and PANC-1 cells were treated with maca preparations alone or combined with DOX. Cell viability, apoptosis-associated signaling, survival-related proteins, lipid droplet accumulation, and lipid metabolism-related proteins were evaluated. Drug interactions were assessed using Bliss independence and Highest Single Agent (HSA) models. Interaction profiles differed among cell lines and depended on the tested maca preparation and DOX concentration. The strongest favorable interactions were observed in PANC-1 cells treated with MR or MB plus 2.5 µM DOX (Bliss/HSA scores: 18.9/13.1 and 17.6/12.4, respectively), whereas BxPC-3 cells showed favorable interactions with MY, MR, and MB at 5 µM DOX (Bliss/HSA scores: 12.4/9.8, 10.7/8.5, and 11.9/9.2, respectively). MIA PaCa-2 cells showed mainly neutral or less-than-additive interactions. These responses were accompanied by changes in caspase-3 activation, PI3K, FAP, and FOXO1 protein levels, lipid droplet accumulation, and ATGL, ABHD5, and PLIN3 levels. Overall, the tested MY, MR, and MB preparations differentially modified pancreatic cancer cell responses to DOX and were associated with distinct survival-related and lipid metabolism-related changes. Further phytochemical characterization and functional mechanistic studies are required to identify the constituents involved and determine whether the observed molecular changes contribute causally to these effects.

items.title: High Intratumoral PROS1 Expression Is Associated with Improved Survival, Reduced Hypoxia Score Markers, and Alterations in Gene Expression Associated with Oncogene Signaling and Cell Cycle Signaling in Selected Solid Tumors.
items.abstract: Protein S (PS), encoded by PROS1, is a vitamin K-dependent physiological anticoagulant with emerging, context-dependent roles in tumor biology. In pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), exogenous PS suppresses tumor growth and intratumoral hypoxia in preclinical models. Notably, high intratumoral PROS1 expression is associated with improved survival and attenuation of oncogenic, hypoxia-responsive, and EMT-related transcriptional programs in PDAC. Here, we examined associations between intratumoral PROS1 expression and overall survival, hypoxia-associated signaling, and genomic instability across nine cancer types using publicly available cBioPortal datasets. Tumors were stratified by low versus high PROS1 expression. Genomic instability was assessed using tumor mutational burden, aneuploidy, and tumor break load, where available. High PROS1 expression was associated with improved survival in ovarian serous cystadenocarcinoma and lung adenocarcinoma in exploratory, unadjusted Mantel-Haenszel hazard ratio analyses. It was also inversely associated with genomic instability markers in ovarian, lung adenocarcinoma, and PDAC. Meta-analyses in select genes under low and high PROS1 expression conditions revealed shifts in pathways linked to oncogenic signaling, cell-cycle regulation, hypoxia, and EMT. Collectively, these findings position PROS1 as a candidate prognostic biomarker in selected cancers and support further investigation of PROS1's roles in limiting tumor progression and preserving genomic stability.

items.title: Treatment Strategies and Future Directions for Locally Advanced Pancreatic Cancer.
items.abstract: Locally advanced pancreatic cancer is a complex clinical entity, combining a locally aggressive tumor in a disease marked by systemic failure. Accordingly, systemic therapy upfront is recommended, with translation of recent advances in the metastatic setting promising to revolutionize the care of locally advanced disease in the future. In those patients where systemic disease remains controlled, locoregional therapies including surgery and radiation may play a role. Specific considerations of these therapies are presented in a disease phenotype marked by invasion into surrounding vasculature/luminal organs. Ongoing investigations are set to define the role of novel therapies in locally advanced disease, some of which have already gained approval. With recent advances in the control of systemic disease, locally advanced disease represents a prime target for study and treatment optimization to improve outcomes for patients.

items.title: The Association Between Asthma and Pancreatic Cancer: A Systematic Review.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Pancreatic cancer is an aggressive malignancy, largely due to its vague clinical presentation and delayed diagnosis. Knowledge of the risk factors is essential to combat this disease. Increasing interest has been directed toward immune-related disorders and their effect on pancreatic cancer development. Studies have investigated the relationship between asthma and pancreatic cancer; however, findings are inconsistent, with some studies reporting a protective association, while others failed to detect any differences. In light of these inconsistent findings, we conducted a systematic review of the available literature to clarify the link between asthma and pancreatic cancer.
METHODS: We identified studies published from 1978 through December 2025 that investigated the association between asthma and pancreatic cancer using PubMed, Scopus, and Embase databases, searched on 2 February 2026. Eligible studies were English-language comparative studies evaluating the association between asthma and pancreatic cancer, including case-control and cohort studies. Eligible outcomes were pancreatic cancer incidence or pancreatic cancer mortality. Studies that did not assess both asthma and pancreatic cancer were excluded. Studies were classified by design, assessed for bias and quality using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale, and presented as a narrative review. This review was reported in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) reporting guideline.
RESULTS: A total of 27 studies were included, comprising 14 case-control studies and 13 cohort studies. Overall, the available literature demonstrates discordant findings regarding the association between asthma and pancreatic cancer. While some studies suggest a potential inverse relationship, others report a null or even positive association.
CONCLUSIONS: The current evidence on the association between asthma and pancreatic cancer remains inconsistent. The discrepancies across studies likely reflect variations in study design, differences in asthma ascertainment, and inconsistent adjustment for established confounders. Future studies with objective asthma diagnosis and adequate confounder control are warranted to clarify this association.

items.title: Corrigendum to: Targeting Glutamine Metabolic Reprogramming in Pancreatic Cancer: Current Insights and Future Directions.
items.abstract: Following publication of the article entitled "Targeting Glutamine Metabolic Reprogramming in Pancreatic Cancer: Cur-rent Insights and Future Directions" [1], certain phrases and expressions were identified that were unclear or inconsistent with established scientific terminology. To ensure the accuracy and clarity of the published record, these expressions have been corrected using appropriate terminology that more accurately conveys the intended scientific meaning. These corrections are limited to the wording and terminology of the affected passages and do not alter the data, results, scientific interpretations, or conclusions of the article. The specific corrections are provided below: Section, Abstract, Original text: However, some studies have shown that inhibitors of this pathway can sensitize PC cells to chemotherapeutic agents, and this synergistic effect provides new insights into the combination therapy for PC. Corrected text: However, some studies have shown that inhibitors of this pathway can sensitize PC cells to chemotherapeutic agents, and this synergistic effect provides new opportunities for developing combination therapies for PC treatment. The original article has been updated accordingly. This corrigendum is published to maintain transparency and accuracy of the scholarly record. The corrected version of the article is available online at: https://www.eurekaselect.com/article/146023 The authors regret these errors and apologise for any inconvenience they may have caused.

items.title: PRMT1 blockade reverts resistance to KRAS (G12C) inhibition through modulating ferroptosis signalling.
items.abstract: While Kirsten rat sarcoma virus (KRAS) G12C inhibitors (KRAS G12Ci) are successful in clinical practice, their long‑term efficacy is limited by acquired resistance, and effective combination strategies are urgently needed. In the present study, pancreatic and lung cancer cell lines resistant to KRAS G12Ci (AMG510/D‑1553) were established. Ribonucleic acid‑sequencing (RNA‑seq) identified significant alterations in ferroptosis‑related signaling in KRAS G12Ci‑resistant cells. Through in vivo and in vitro experiments, it was found that an increase occurred in the expression level of protein arginine methyltransferase 1 (PRMT1) in resistant cells. The combined inhibition of KRAS G12C and PRMT1 showed a stronger inhibitory effect on tumor growth than single‑target inhibition. Mechanistically, the inhibition of PRMT1 could make histone H4 at arginine 3 (H4R3me2a) less enriched in the promoter region of solute carrier family 7 member 11 (SLC7A11). This suggests that PRMT1 may promote the transcription of SLC7A11 via epigenetic regulation mediated by H4R3me2a. Thus, this inhibits ferroptosis and potentially contributes to the maintenance of the KRAS G12Ci‑resistant phenotype. In summary, elevated PRMT1 expression was associated with KRAS G12C inhibitor resistance, and pharmacological inhibition of PRMT1‑associated activity enhanced the efficacy of KRAS G12C inhibition partly through ferroptosis. Further genetic validation is required to establish the specific role of PRMT1. The results of the present study will provide new targets and a theoretical basis for overcoming KRAS‑targeted treatment resistance, and will also promote the clinical translation of combined therapy.

items.title: Immune cell metabolic reprogramming in pancreatic cancer: roles in tumor progression and therapeutic strategies.
items.abstract: Pancreatic cancer is one of the most lethal malignancies of the digestive system, and its profoundly immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME) represents a major driver of tumor progression and therapeutic resistance. Emerging evidence indicates that metabolic reprogramming profoundly influences the polarization, effector function, survival, and fate of immune cells within the TME, thereby shaping the balance between antitumor immunity and immune escape. However, substantial challenges remain, including the incompletely understood metabolic heterogeneity among distinct immune cell subsets and the limited clinical translation of therapeutic strategies combining metabolic intervention with immunotherapy. In this review, we summarize the metabolic reprogramming characteristics and underlying molecular mechanisms of major immune cell populations in pancreatic cancer, including T cells, tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs), myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs), and natural killer (NK) cells, with particular emphasis on their reciprocal interactions with pancreatic cancer progression and the immunosuppressive microenvironment. We further discuss recent advances in metabolism-targeted therapies and immunotherapy, highlighting the therapeutic potential of combination strategies centered on immunometabolic modulation. Finally, we outline current challenges and emerging opportunities in this rapidly evolving field, with the aim of providing a mechanistic framework and translational perspectives for the development of precision therapeutic strategies for pancreatic cancer.

items.title: Multi-targeted Mechanisms of Erianin against Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma: Integrative Network Pharmacology, Bioinformatics, and Experimental Validation.
items.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Erianin is a natural benzyl compound extracted from Dendrobium drumbium. However, the mechanism of action of Erianin against pancreatic cancer (PC) is still unclear. The aim of this study was to systematically elucidate the therapeutic potential of Erianin in PC and its molecular mechanisms.
METHODS: The potential therapeutic targets of Erianin in the treatment of PC were identified through online databases. The GeneMANIA database was used to expand the network pharmacology (NP) analysis results. The "Clinical Home" platform and GEPIA2 database were used to clarify the clinical significance of the key targets. Furthermore, protein-protein interaction (PPI), molecular docking, kinetic simulation, and enrichment analysis were used to predict the core targets and potential mechanisms of Erianin against PC. Finally, NP prediction results were confirmed by in vitro cell experiments.
RESULTS: A total of 10 hub genes, such as ESR1, HSP90AA1, HIF1A, ERBB2, ALB, NFKB1, SRC, PIK3CA, PPARG, and HARS, were identified by functional association of NP using the gene- MANIA database (GMFA). These targets were significantly enriched in PI3K-Akt and MAPK signaling pathways, and Erianin had a strong binding ability with key targets. In vitro experiments showed that Erianin significantly inhibited the proliferation, migration, and invasion of PC cells. The expression of hub genes was downregulated by Erianin, and Erianin inhibited the activation of the PI3K/AKT/MAPK pathway.
DISCUSSION: In the PI3K-Akt signaling pathway, in addition to core targets, related genes such as IRS1, GRB2, and HRAS were additionally identified, further refining the target network through which erianin exerts its antitumor effects via this pathway. Cell-level experimental results strongly validated the predictions from network pharmacology and bioinformatics. CCK8 proliferation assays, colony formation assays, wound healing assays, and Transwell invasion assays showed that Erianin significantly inhibited the proliferation, migration, and invasion abilities of pancreatic cancer cells in a dose-dependent manner. qRT-PCR results revealed that Erianin could downregulate the expression levels of multiple key genes, such as HSP90AA1, CCND1, and ERBB2, which are closely associated with the previously predicted targets and signaling pathways.
CONCLUSION: Erianin exerted a multi-target effect against PC through the PI3K/Akt/MAPK signaling pathway and the key genes PIK3CA, HIF1A, and ERBB2, providing a theoretical basis for further clinical research on Erianin.

items.title: FGFBP2 p.T186S mutation in tumor associated fibroblasts supports progression of pancreatic cancer through autocrine and paracrine mechanisms.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Pancreatic cancer is one of the most aggressive human tumors with an extremely poor prognosis. The tumor microenvironment is characterized by a complex network of cellular interactions, in which cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) play a pivotal role in the initiation and progression of the disease. Previously identified somatic cancer-associated fibroblast (CAF) mutations may have functional consequences thereby affecting pancreatic cancer biology. One of the identified mutations of the fibroblast growth factor binding protein 2 gene (FGFBP2) causes replacement from threonine to serine (p.T186S). The aim of this study was to investigate how this mutation may affect fibroblast function, the tumor microenvironment and cancer progression.
METHODS: FGFBP2 p.T186S mutation harboring fibroblasts (FGFBP2MUT) and wild-type fibroblasts (FGFBP2WT) were analyzed for activation markers, viable cell numbers, and migration. PANC-1 pancreatic cancer cells were incubated with conditioned media from FGFBP2MUT and FGFBP2WT fibroblasts to assess viable cell numbers and signaling pathway activation. RNA sequencing was performed to identify differentially expressed genes. Furthermore, publicly available single-cell RNA sequencing and spatial transcriptomic datasets were analyzed to explore downstream molecular mechanisms.
RESULTS: FGFBP2 p.T186S mutation harboring cells (FGFBP2MUT) displayed increased expression of activation markers and cytokines as compared to controls. FGFBP2MUT cells exhibited increased viable cell numbers and migration. Further, conditioned medium derived from FGFBP2MUT promoted growth of the pancreatic cancer cell line PANC-1 and resulted in increased activation of the ERK1/2 signaling pathway. RNA sequencing analysis of PANC-1 cells treated with conditioned media derived from FGFBP2MUT revealed upregulation of the ETS homologous factor (EHF) gene. Single-cell RNA sequencing analysis showed that EHF was primarily expressed in tumor cells and regulated fibroblasts through the platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF) signaling pathway. In addition, spatial transcriptomic analysis revealed a correlation between EHF expression and CAF markers ACTA2, POSTN, and COL1A1.
CONCLUSIONS: Our study shows that the FGFBP2 p.T186S point mutation promotes fibroblast activation potentially influencing tumor progression by increasing the viable cell population of pancreatic cancer cells.

items.title: Identification and characterization of a novel fungal pyranose 2-oxidase from the Punctularia strigosozonata with potent cytotoxicity against pancreatic carcinoma cell lines.
items.abstract: Pyranose oxidase (POx) is a FAD-dependent oxidoreductase that catalyzes the oxidation of D-glucose to 2-keto-D-glucose with concomitant production of hydrogen peroxide (H2O2). Although POx has been well characterized in several fungi and bacteria, its potential in cancer therapy remains largely unexplored. In this study, we identified a novel pyranose 2-oxidase, designated PsPOx, from the wood-decaying fungus Punctularia strigosozonata through gene mining. The gene was codon-optimized, synthesized, and heterologously expressed in Escherichia coli. The recombinant enzyme was purified and biochemically characterized. Sequence alignment and structural modeling confirmed that PsPOx possesses all conserved features of the GMC superfamily. Kinetic analysis showed that PsPOx exhibits the highest catalytic efficiency (k cat/K m = 85.09 mM-1 s-1) towards D-glucose, with a K m value of 0.8375 mM, indicating a strong substrate affinity. Using the CCK-8 assay, PsPOx demonstrated potent dose-dependent cytotoxicity against three human pancreatic carcinoma cell lines (PANC-1, AsPC-1, and BxPC-3), with IC50 values of 257.8, 195.2, and 176.2 ng mL-1, respectively. However, the IC50 value for the normal human pancreatic epithelial cell line hTERT-HPNE was 195.6 ng mL-1, which was comparable to those for AsPC-1 and BxPC-3, indicating that free PsPOx lacks selectivity between tumor and normal cells. Mechanistic studies revealed that PsPOx treatment increased intracellular and mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels, induced G0/G1 cell cycle arrest, downregulated Cyclin D1 and PCNA expression, and triggered apoptosis in BxPC-3 cells. These results preliminarily demonstrate that PsPOx possesses antitumor activity in vitro and may serve as a candidate for further development.

items.title: Anlotinib Plus S-1 in Advanced Pancreatic Cancer: Efficacy, Safety, and Relevance to Chronic Cancer Care.
items.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the clinical efficacy and tolerability of anlotinib combined with S-1 for advanced pancreatic carcinoma.
STUDY DESIGN: A retrospective study. Place and Duration of the Study: Department of Oncology, Zhenjiang First People's Hospital, Jiangsu, China, from January 2022 to December 2024.
METHODOLOGY: Fifty cases with metastatic pancreatic cancer who had received at least one line of chemotherapy were enrolled. The anlotinib group received anlotinib combined with S-1, while the chemotherapy group received S-1 alone. Tumour response evaluated according to RECIST criteria was categorised as complete response (CR), partial response (PR), stable disease (SD) and progressive disease (PD). All categorical efficacy endpoints, together with derived endpoints including objective response rate (ORR) and disease control rate (DCR), were presented as n (%). Between-group comparisons of tumour response and clinicopathological characteristics were conducted using the chi-square test. The Kaplan-Meier method was adopted for progression-free survival (PFS) analysis.
RESULTS: Of the enrolled patients, the median age was 58 years, and 37 (74%) patients were male. Compared with the chemotherapy‑ alone group, the anlotinib group showed numerically better short-term efficacy: ORR was 5 (25.0%) vs. 3 (10.0%), DCR was 11 (55.0%) vs. 11 (36.7%). Moreover, anlotinib combination therapy conferred survival benefits. The median PFS was 4.5 months vs. 2.3 months (HR = 0.38 [95% CI: 0.21 to 0.68], p <0.05). The incidence of any-grade adverse reactions in the anlotinib group was 5 (25%), with no ≥ grade 3 adverse events reported, and no unreported safety events occurred.
CONCLUSION: Anlotinib combined with S-1 shows favourable efficacy in the subsequent-line treatment of metastatic pancreatic cancer without increasing the risk of chemotherapy-related adverse reactions. In the context of chronic disease management, this scheme can be selected for subsequent-line treatment of metastatic pancreatic cancer.
KEY WORDS: Pancreatic cancer, Anlotinib, S-1, Efficacy, Progression-free survival.

items.title: Exploratory mendelian randomization of circulating metabolites and multi-omics characterization of ERCC1 in pancreatic cancer.
items.abstract: Pancreatic cancer remains highly lethal, and reliable metabolic and molecular markers for risk stratification and prognosis are limited. We investigated potential associations between circulating metabolites and pancreatic cancer risk and further evaluated the biological and prognostic relevance of prioritized candidate genes. We assessed 233 circulating metabolites using two-sample Mendelian randomization. Gene annotation, polygenic prioritization, summary-data-based Mendelian randomization, and Bayesian colocalization were used to prioritize candidate genes. Transcriptomic, proteomic, pathway, survival, and single-cell analyses were integrated with experimental validation, including Western blotting, gene knockdown, colony formation, wound-healing, Transwell migration, and immunohistochemistry. Fifteen circulating metabolites showed nominal Mendelian randomization association signals with pancreatic cancer risk. The free cholesterol-to-total lipids ratio in large very-low-density lipoprotein and saturated fatty acids showed relatively consistent inverse association patterns across multiple methods, whereas several other lipid-related traits showed method-specific exploratory signals. Excision repair cross-complementation group 1 (ERCC1) was prioritized as a candidate for further biological investigation. Colocalization did not support a shared causal variant between ERCC1 expression and pancreatic cancer risk, suggesting that ERCC1 should not be interpreted as a genetically confirmed mediator. The observed ERCC1-related metabolite associations therefore remained hypothesis-generating rather than evidence of an established genetic or metabolic mechanism. ERCC1 expression was increased in pancreatic cancer tissues and selected pancreatic cancer cell lines, associated with poorer prognosis, and enriched in malignant epithelial and cancer-associated fibroblast compartments. ERCC1 knockdown reduced clonogenic growth and migratory phenotypes, and immunohistochemistry showed stronger ERCC1 staining in pancreatic cancer tissues than in adjacent normal tissues in three paired specimens. Additional exploratory evaluation of the Cox-weighted prognostic score showed variable predictive performance in CPTAC-PDC000270 and E-MTAB-6134, with 1-, 2-, and 3-year AUCs of 0.658, 0.731, and 0.627 and 0.610, 0.607, and 0.553, respectively. This integrative analysis highlights lipid-related metabolic traits and provided expression-based and preliminary functional evidence supporting further investigation of ERCC1 in pancreatic cancer. Further mechanistic studies and lipidomic validation are warranted.

items.title: Vaccinia-related kinase 2 confers pancreatic cancer with gemcitabine resistance through TPI1-driven aerobic glycolysis.
items.abstract: Gemcitabine(GEM)-based chemotherapy is considered the first-line regimen for pancreatic cancer(PC), but the poor responsiveness and chemoresistance greatly limit its application. Metabolic reprogramming, especially aerobic glycolysis, which is regulated by glycolytic enzymes, is closely associated with the malignant behavior of PC. Recently, triosephosphate isomerase 1(TPI1), as a key glycolytic enzyme involved in glycolysis, was reported to be increased in GEM-treated PC patients with poor outcome whereas the mechanism remains unclear. In this study, we identified vaccinia-related kinase 2 (VRK2), a serine/threonine protein kinase, which was upregulated in GEM-resistant PC cells and conferred GEM resistance by promoting TPI1-driven aerobic glycolysis. Further studies showed that phosphorylation and nuclear translocation of the transcriptional factor SP1 induced by VRK2 contributed to the interaction of SP1 with the promoter region of TPI1 and thus enhanced the transcriptional activity of TPI1. Taken together, our findings uncover a novel role for VRK2 in modulating glycolytic reprogramming and GEM-resistance, which implicates VRK2 as a potential therapeutic target in PC.

items.title: Natural history and pancreatic cancer risk in PRSS1-associated hereditary pancreatitis: a nationwide cohort.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND AND AIMS: Hereditary pancreatitis caused by pathogenic variants in the cationic trypsinogen gene is associated with early pancreatic injury and increased pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma risk, but current estimates rely on small historical cohorts. We reassessed the natural history, penetrance, and long-term cancer risk in a nationwide genetically confirmed cohort.
METHODS: We conducted a retrospective nationwide cohort study including individuals identified with PRSS1 variants associated with hereditary pancreatitis in France between 1996 and 2025 through the three national reference laboratories. Among 718 identified carriers, 455 had available follow-up. Clinical data were collected using a standardized electronic case report form. Outcomes included pancreatic exocrine insufficiency, diabetes mellitus, and pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma. Standardized incidence and mortality ratios were calculated using national population data.
RESULTS: Median age at symptom onset was 12.5 years (interquartile range, 6.8-24.3), and overall penetrance was 77.6%. The cumulative risk of pancreatic exocrine insufficiency reached 27.5% (95% CI, 22.5-32.5) at age 50 years and 36.2% (95% CI, 30.2-42.2) at age 60 years; corresponding estimates for diabetes mellitus were 20.4% (95% CI, 15.2-25.5) and 27.2% (95% CI, 21.1-33.4), respectively. Twenty-two individuals developed pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma at a median age of 63.8 years (interquartile range, 52.3-73.6), with cumulative risk by ages 50 and 60 years of 2.0% (95% CI, 0.2-3.9) and 5.9% (95% CI, 2.3-9.6), respectively. The age- and sex-adjusted standardized incidence ratio for pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma was 32.2 (95% CI, 19.4-50.3). Diabetes mellitus was independently associated with an increased risk of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (hazard ratio, 6.8; 95% CI, 2.1-21.2). Overall mortality was higher than in the general population (standardized mortality ratio, 3.2; 95% CI, 2.4-4.3).
CONCLUSIONS: In this nationwide cohort with nearly three decades of follow-up, PRSS1-associated hereditary pancreatitis showed high penetrance, early pancreatic insufficiency, and markedly increased pancreatic cancer risk. These findings support lifelong follow-up and pancreatic cancer surveillance strategies that account for increasing risk with age and substantial interindividual variability in age at diagnosis.

items.title: Awareness of the signs and symptoms of pancreatic cancer: a cross-sectional study from a developing country setting.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Pancreatic cancer (PC) is associated with poor prognosis, largely due to delayed diagnosis and limited awareness of its risk factors, symptoms, and diagnostic approaches. This study aimed to assess public awareness, knowledge, and attitudes toward PC among adults.
METHODS: A cross-sectional study was conducted among 438 adults using a structured, validated questionnaire administered through face-to-face interviews. Participants' awareness, knowledge of risk factors and diagnostic methods, attitudes toward seeking medical care, and screening practices were assessed. Multivariate analysis was performed to identify independent predictors of PC awareness.
RESULTS: Among the 438 participants, 73.7% had heard of PC, and 98.6% recognized it as a serious disease. However, knowledge remained limited, particularly regarding symptoms and diagnostic approaches. Alcohol consumption (72.4%), chronic pancreatitis (65.5%), and family history (65.1%) were commonly recognized risk factors, while misconceptions regarding radiation exposure (34.5%) were evident. More than 70% of participants were unaware of PC diagnostic methods. Despite generally positive health-seeking attitudes, with 60.3% reporting that they would be very likely to consult a physician if they experienced alarming symptoms, only 2.7% had undergone screening, and 83.6% had never received information about PC from a healthcare provider. Multivariate analysis identified no independent predictors of PC awareness.
CONCLUSION: Although general awareness of PC was moderate and attitudes toward seeking medical care were positive, substantial knowledge gaps persisted regarding symptoms, risk factors, and diagnostic approaches. These findings highlight the need for targeted, evidence-based educational interventions integrated into primary healthcare and chronic disease management services to improve public understanding, promote timely medical consultation, and potentially reduce diagnostic delays.

items.title: Aptamer-functionalized exosomes co-delivering miR-934 inhibitor and gemcitabine for targeted pancreatic cancer therapy.
items.abstract: Pancreatic cancer remains a malignancy with limited treatment efficacy and high resistance to chemotherapy. miR-934 was identified as an oncogenic miRNA significantly upregulated in pancreatic cancer, promoting tumor progression, epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT), and chemoresistance by targeting the tumor suppressor PRUNE2. Inhibition of miR-934 sensitized cancer cells to Gemcitabine (GEM)-induced apoptosis, highlighting its therapeutic potential. To enhance delivery efficiency, AS1411 (oligonucleotide aptamer of nucleolin)-functionalized exosomes were engineered to co-deliver miR-934 inhibitor and GEM. The functionalized exosomes demonstrated high encapsulation efficiency, enhanced cellular uptake and tumor-targeting capability, and improved suppression of malignant phenotypes. This platform not only suppressed cell migration, invasion, and EMT but also enhanced GEM-induced apoptosis by restoring PRUNE2 expression and activating pro-apoptotic pathways. Furthermore, PRUNE2 overexpression reversed the malignant phenotypes and gemcitabine resistance induced by miR-934, further confirming the critical role of the miR-934/PRUNE2 axis in pancreatic cancer progression. In vivo, AS1411-functionalized engineered exosomes co-delivering miR-934 inhibitor and gemcitabine exhibited enhanced tumor accumulation and significantly suppressed tumor growth compared with free drug treatment and non-functionalized exosomes. These findings underscore the potential of aptamer-functionalized exosomes as a targeted therapeutic strategy for pancreatic cancer by integrating miRNA modulation and chemotherapeutic delivery.

items.title: Agrimoniin combines with erlotinib to inhibit the proliferation of pancreatic cancer cells by suppressing signal interactions in the tumor microenvironment and disrupting two positive feedback loops involving lactic acid production.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Erlotinib, an epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) small molecule inhibitor approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for the treatment of pancreatic cancer, faces significant drug resistance challenges. To address this, we investigated the potential of agrimoniin, a key active compound in the traditional Chinese medicine Agrimonia pilosa, which is known for its potent anticancer activity. This study aims to explore the combined effect of these two compounds in pancreatic cancer.
METHODS: We sought to verify the combined inhibitory effect of pancreatic cancer by agrimoniin and erlotinib in vitro and in vivo using various assays, including subcutaneous xenograft experiments and western blot. Single-cell RNA sequencing, bioinformatics, western blot, and lactic acid assays were performed to study how agrimoniin and erlotinib affect the tumor microenvironment and aerobic glycolysis. Finally, using signal pathway inhibitors/agonists, lactic acid assays, and Western blot, we aimed to reveal two positive feedback loops between signal pathways and lactic acid production.
RESULTS: Agrimoniin combines with erlotinib to inhibit proliferation of pancreatic cancer cells. Together, they effectively suppress signal interactions between tumor cells, stromal cells, and macrophages within subcutaneous tumors. Simultaneously, they jointly inhibit aerobic glycolysis and lactic acid production in pancreatic cancer. Notably, this study proposes two potentially novel positive feedback loops between the PI3K/AKT/HIF-1α/HK2, MEK/ERK/HIF-1α/HK2 signaling pathways and lactic acid production.
CONCLUSIONS: The combination of agrimoniin and erlotinib suppresses signal interactions between tumor cells, macrophages, and stromal cells in the tumor microenvironment, reprograms aerobic glycolysis, disrupts two positive feedback loops, thereby cooperatively inhibiting the proliferation of pancreatic cancer cells. This study provides a theoretical basis for agrimoniin as a sensitizer or resistance-reversing agent for erlotinib, and offers new insights and potential targets for pancreatic cancer drug development.

items.title: A Library of Potent TCRs Derived from Healthy Donors Targeting Kras G12d and G12v Neoantigens.
items.abstract: Kirsten rat sarcoma (KRAS), the most frequently altered oncogene, is a key target for T cell-based therapies. Mutant KRAS (mKRAS)-specific T cell receptors (TCRs) enable targeted treatment for patients with matching mKRAS/HLA allele pairs. We generated a TCR warehouse library covering approximately one-quarter of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma patients and 10% of colorectal cancer patients. Warehouse TCRs exhibit strong avidities and cytotoxicity, comparable to existing benchmark TCRs. Detailed characterization of each TCR revealed unique biology for specific KRAS neoantigens. TCRs with high sensitivity for KRAS G12V/HLA-C*01:02 also recognize the wild-type epitope. However, the wild-type epitope abundance appears to be significantly lower, potentially creating a therapeutic window, albeit necessitating deeper evaluation. Additionally, we show that TCRs recognize KRAS G12V on HLA-C*03:03 and HLA-C*03:04 interchangeably, thereby resulting in a single neoantigen with one of the highest frequencies. In summary, this mKRAS-targeted TCR library comprises candidates for further preclinical and clinical development.

items.title: Three cases of pancreatectomy for locally advanced pancreatic cancer with arterial aberrations: case series and literature review.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Locally advanced pancreatic cancer has traditionally been considered unresectable in the presence of major vascular involvement. However, advances in vascular resection and reconstruction techniques have expanded the surgical options for selected patients and may allow radical resection in cases previously considered unresectable.
CASES: We present three cases of locally advanced pancreatic adenocarcinoma associated with vascular involvement and hepatic arterial anatomical variations. Two patients had involvement of the portal vein and common hepatic artery, while the third had suspected involvement of the superior mesenteric artery (SMA) at its origin. All three patients had anatomical arterial variations. The first patient, a 64-year-old woman, had a Michels type VII variation, whereas the second and third patients had Michels type IX variations. Two patients successfully underwent pancreaticoduodenectomy with combined venous and arterial resection and reconstruction. In the third case, intraoperative exploration revealed perivascular fibrosis without true invasion of the SMA, thereby avoiding the need for arterial resection and reconstruction.
CONCLUSION: Combined arterial and venous resection and reconstruction may be feasible in carefully selected patients with locally advanced pancreatic cancer and may facilitate radical resection in selected cases. Careful preoperative assessment of celiac and mesenteric arterial anatomy and recognition of arterial variations are essential for surgical planning and may help reduce the risk of vascular injury and perioperative morbidity.
